material_claims.statement: In run mode noscope revokes every credential it minted before the noscope process exits. This applies when the child exits normally, when the child cannot start, and when a shutdown signal arrives.

The run supervisor forwards a shutdown signal to the child, triggers revocation once, and returns the child exit status to the caller. A second revocation must not run after a signal already caused one.

noscope registers handlers for SIGTERM, SIGINT and SIGHUP in run mode and forwards each of them to the child. A second shutdown signal escalates to SIGKILL, and noscope then reports exit status 128 plus the signal number.
When a shutdown signal arrives, noscope tries to revoke every active credential. It reports each provider failure on stderr. The run still finishes with the child exit status.

When any provider fails during a multi-provider mint in run mode, noscope revokes the credentials that already succeeded. It then fails with a configuration error. The error names each failed provider and its reason.

A rollback revocation retries a failed attempt with delays that start at 100 milliseconds and double each time. Retries stop after 3 retries, when the 5 second budget runs out, or when an attempt times out. A zero budget disables revocation completely.
Every rollback revocation attempt writes one log line to stderr. The line names the credential id, the provider, the expiry, the attempt number, and the reason when the attempt failed.

A revoke call runs the provider revoke command with the opaque token id in the environment and never the secret value. Exit status zero means success. Any other exit status, a missing revoke command, an empty revoke command, or a spawn failure is a provider error that names the provider.
Each revoke attempt emits a start event, then either a success event or a failure event. Each event names the provider, the token id, and the elapsed time.
The revoke command takes the credential to revoke either from the --token-id and --provider flags or from a mint envelope read on standard input. It never accepts the secret token value.
The mint command refuses to write the credential envelope when standard output is a terminal. The operator must pass --force-terminal to override the refusal.
The mint command writes a JSON array of credential envelopes to standard output. It writes the same JSON whatever value --output carries.

Command results go to standard output and diagnostics go to standard error. Errors, runtime events, rollback logs and the human doctor report all use standard error, so a caller can pipe stdout safely.

When a command fails and --output json is set, noscope writes one JSON object to standard error. The object carries the status, the command name, the error class and the message. In text mode it writes one line that starts with 'noscope: '.

The process exit status tells the caller which class of failure happened. Usage and security failures give 64. Provider failures give 65. Profile failures give 66. Internal failures give 70. Configuration failures give 78. Success gives 0.
In run mode the noscope exit status is the child exit status. noscope does not replace a child status with its own status when the child ran and exited.
noscope gives minted credentials to the child process only through environment variables. An injected credential variable replaces any inherited variable that has the same name.
When the operator names providers on the command line, each credential lands in the environment variable <PROVIDER>_TOKEN, with the provider name in upper case.

A profile names one or more credentials. Each credential gets the environment variable stated in the profile, or <PROVIDER>_TOKEN_<index> when the profile states none. Two credentials from the same provider resolve that provider only once.
The --profile flag is a complete alternative to --provider, --role and --ttl. noscope rejects a command that mixes them, and rejects a run or mint command that supplies neither form.

Before any provider process starts, noscope checks the request. It must name at least one provider. The role must be non-empty and free of shell metacharacters. The time to live must be greater than zero.
noscope disables core dumps before it handles any credential material. A command aborts with a security error when the platform refuses to disable them.

Provider settings resolve by strict precedence: command line flags beat NOSCOPE_ environment variables, which beat the provider config file. The winning layer supplies all commands, and layers never merge.

noscope runs the provider mint command with the environment the provider config declares. It adds the provider name in NOSCOPE_PROVIDER and the role in NOSCOPE_ROLE. It replaces the role and time-to-live placeholders first.
noscope bounds every provider process. A mint or revoke command has 30 seconds to finish and 5 seconds to die after a kill request. At most 8 mint commands run at the same time.
A provider command string that parses to no arguments is a failure that names the provider and the command type. noscope never runs an empty command.

noscope splits a configured command string into arguments using POSIX shell quoting rules. When the quoting is unbalanced it falls back to splitting on whitespace so the caller always receives usable arguments.

Run mode writes lifecycle events for mint and revoke to standard error. The operator selects text or JSON with --log-format, and any other value is a usage error. This choice does not change the --output format.
The validate command reports whether a provider configuration is usable without running any provider command. A failure names the failing command type and its path so the operator can fix it.
The dry-run command shows the provider name, the configuration source, the role and the time to live. It also shows the mint, refresh and revoke commands that would run. It executes nothing.

The doctor command reports one line per local setup check with a pass, warning or failure marker, plus a count summary. It exits 0 when all checks pass, 1 when only warnings occur, and 78 when any check fails.
The init command creates the noscope config directory and its providers and profiles subdirectories. Re-running it changes nothing and says so, and it succeeds either way.
The doctor and init commands look for configuration under XDG_CONFIG_HOME. When that variable is unset they use the .config directory inside HOME.
noscope generates shell completions for bash, zsh and fish on standard output.
Asking for help or the version writes to standard output and exits 0. An unparseable command line writes the usage error and exits 2.
Help text speaks to operators. It carries concrete run, mint and revoke examples, explains that --profile excludes the credential flags, and never shows internal rule identifiers.
noscope refuses a revoke command line that carries a raw --token flag, because process arguments are visible to other users. The opaque --token-id flag stays allowed.
noscope exposes one public error type. Every command failure carries a class, a message and an exit code drawn from that single type.

unsupported_recommendations.recommendation: The mint command should roll back credentials that already succeeded when a later provider in the same batch fails, as run mode does. Rationale: cmd_mint propagates the CredentialSetError at src/main.rs:725 with no rollback, while cmd_run rolls back at line 190. The asymmetry looks like a leak, but no code or test states the intended mint behaviour.

A role or time to live taken from a profile file should get the same validation as one taken from the command line. Rationale: resolve_profile_specs_and_providers never calls Client::validate_mint, so profile roles skip the shell-metacharacter check. Nothing states whether profile files are trusted input.

noscope should be able to tell an operator whether a non-zero exit came from the child or from noscope itself. Rationale: Child codes 0-255 and noscope sysexits codes 0-78 share the same range with no marker, but no code or comment addresses the collision.

Runtime events for mint and revoke should reach stderr for every command, not only for run. Rationale: Only cmd_run installs a runtime emitter, so execute_revoke's events are dropped for standalone revoke. No test or comment states whether that silence is deliberate.

The rollback budget field named revoke_timeout is meant to bound one attempt, not the whole retry sequence. Rationale: The doc comment at src/credential_set.rs:148 says per attempt, while revoke_token_with_budget uses it as a total wall clock budget. Which reading is intended is not recorded anywhere.

The 20 millisecond poll interval in the run supervision loop bounds how long a shutdown signal waits before it reaches the child. Rationale: src/main.rs:407 sleeps 20ms per pass, but no requirement or test states a latency target, so this is an implementation choice rather than an obligation.

uncertainty.rationale: Single-pass extraction from a codebase with substantial dead and test-only code; reachability judgments were later checked by the adversarial pass.

open_questions: Does a SIGKILL of noscope itself leave credentials live until TTL expiry, as README 'planned' notes suggest?
RunSignalWiring in src/run_signal_wiring.rs holds the revoke_attempted flag, so the once-only guarantee is shared with that module.
The escalation policy itself lives in src/run_signal_wiring.rs and src/signal_policy.rs, so no single symbol here owns it.
A revoke failure at shutdown is only printed, never reflected in the exit status. Is that intended?
cmd_mint propagates the same failure at src/main.rs:725 with no rollback, so mint mode appears to leak the succeeded credentials.
RollbackBudget.revoke_timeout is documented as a per-attempt timeout but this function uses it as a total wall-clock budget.
Rollback log lines bypass the runtime event emitter, so --log-format json does not apply to them.
Passing an empty NOSCOPE_TOKEN may be indistinguishable from a real empty token for a provider script.
cmd_revoke installs no runtime emitter, so src/event.rs:300 drops these events for the standalone revoke command.
Clap already enforces the exclusion, so the in-function checks are a second, unreachable guard.
The check runs before provider resolution, so no error ordering issue, but run mode has no equivalent check.
Is ignoring --output text for mint deliberate, or an oversight in the dispatch table?
cmd_doctor puts the text report on stderr but the JSON report on stdout, which is an asymmetry between formats.
The JSON error object is never validated against a schema or asserted by a test in this partition.
A multi-error reports 65, so a mixed batch hides the other classes.
A child exiting 78 is indistinguishable from a noscope configuration failure.
Silent overwrite of an inherited variable gives the operator no warning.
A provider name with a hyphen produces an env key that a shell cannot reference easily.
The profile path never calls validate_mint, so a role from a profile file skips the shell-metacharacter check that a flag role gets.
cli_adapter::check_profile_flag_exclusion has no production caller, so clap is the only live enforcement.
The profile path skips this call entirely, so profile roles and TTLs are unchecked.
Client::new_best_effort at src/client.rs:119 swallows the failure. Does any caller use it in production?
Every CLI handler passes ProviderOverrides::default, so the flags layer is unreachable from the current CLI.
A provider config that sets NOSCOPE_PROVIDER itself is silently overwritten.
ClientOptions carries provider_timeout and max_concurrent, but the handlers hardcode the values instead of reading them.
The whitespace fallback can produce a different argv from what the operator intended, with no warning.
mint and revoke install no emitter, so their mint and revoke events are silently dropped. Is that intended?
The executable check itself lives in provider::validate_provider outside this partition.
The JSON form prints the provider env map, which could expose config-supplied secrets in logs.
Exit 1 is not a sysexits value, so doctor breaks the exit code contract that the other commands follow.
cli.rs describes init as creating directories 'with secure permissions', but the mode is set in doctor.rs, outside this partition.
Both handlers fall back to /root/.config when HOME is also unset, which can point a normal user at the root config.
Exit 2 for a bad command line differs from the 64 that a usage error from the handlers produces.
No production code calls validate_revoke_argv, so the only live rejection is clap's unknown-flag error with exit 2 instead of a security error with exit 64.
Should the CLI call the adapter so the failure class is correct?

material_claims.statement: A multi-provider mint succeeds only when every requested provider returns a credential. If one provider fails, the run produces no credential set and hands back every credential already minted so the caller can revoke it.
The mint orchestration gives each provider its own time budget. A provider that does not answer inside the budget counts as a failed provider, and the failure fails the whole mint.
A provider timeout message names the provider and states the number of seconds that passed, so the operator can see which provider was slow.
The orchestration never runs more provider commands at the same time than the configured concurrency limit. The default limit is 8 providers.
A mint configuration with a concurrency limit of zero is invalid. The system rejects it before it starts any provider command.
The orchestration waits for a result from every requested provider before it decides success or failure. It does not cancel the other providers after the first failure.

Every provider mint attempt reports a start event and then one success or failure event. Each closing event states the provider, the measured duration, and either the credential identifier or the error text.
A successful multi-provider mint prints one JSON array on a single line. The array holds one credential envelope for each minted credential. An empty credential set prints nothing.
Two credentials in one set must not use the same environment variable name. The system rejects such a set and names the environment variable together with every provider that claims it.
A credential set holds live secret material. The system must not copy it, serialise it, or show any secret value in diagnostic output. Diagnostic output shows only the number of credentials.
After a successful mint the child process receives each credential in its own environment variable. The request or the profile chooses that variable name.
Rollback after a failed mint must finish inside a fixed time budget and must make only a limited number of revocation attempts. The default budget is 5 seconds with 3 retries.
Each rollback revocation attempt writes one log line that names the provider, the credential identifier, and the credential expiry time. A failed attempt also states the reason.
Each credential gets its own refresh time, computed from its own expiry. The refresh time always lies between the current time and the expiry time, so no credential refreshes after it expires.
The expiry of one credential must not stop the child process and must not cause a new mint. The system only writes a warning that names the provider and the credential identifier.
A failed credential refresh must never stop the child process. The system retries with growing delays and, once the retries end, lets the current credential expire on its own.
Every refresh failure produces a warning for the operator, even when the system still plans a retry.
The refresh retry schedule starts at 1 second and doubles for each further attempt. It stops after 4 retries. Each delay varies by up to 25 percent.
The retry work after a refresh failure must not use more than half of the credential lifetime that remains. With no lifetime left the system makes no retry at all.
In multi-credential mode the failure count of one credential never changes the failure count or the retry plan of another credential.
A run of failed refreshes never disables refresh for good. After the failure window the credential returns to its normal refresh cadence, and the next attempt waits at least 1 second.
The system runs a refresh command only for credentials whose refresh time has arrived, and only while the child process still runs. After the child exits it runs no further refresh command.
A provider refresh command receives the current credential value, its identifier, and its expiry time, so the provider can renew or replace that exact lease.
After a refresh the system reports whether the provider kept the same credential value or issued a new one. It then clears the failure count for that credential.
When rotate mode is active, the system warns at startup that environment injection happens once at spawn time. The running child does not see refreshed credentials.
The refresh runtime sleeps until the earliest due credential and no longer, so no credential misses its own refresh time.

unsupported_recommendations.recommendation: Mint mode should revoke already minted credentials when a later provider fails, in the same way that run mode does. Rationale: cmd_run rolls back through revoke_run_credentials, while cmd_mint drops the succeeded tokens with `?`. The asymmetry looks unintended, but no code or document states the intent for mint mode.

An empty credential request should be rejected before any provider runs, rather than treated as an empty success. Rationale: validate_credential_specs rejects an empty spec list, while mint_all and resolve_mint_results both return an empty credential set for an empty list. Which side is authoritative is not recorded.

Credential identifiers in emitted events should carry the redacted form rather than the raw provider token id. Rationale: Event::set_token_id documents that the caller must pass a redacted identifier, but mint_all and run_once pass the raw token id. Every other caller does the same, so the doc comment may simply be stale.

The refresh subsystem was built for a rotate mode that the CLI never gained, so its obligations describe a planned feature rather than shipped behaviour. Rationale: No CLI flag, no constructor call, and no wiring test reaches RefreshRuntimeLoop from main. This is a reading of the gap, not something any line of code states.

The rollback time budget should cover the whole set of minted credentials, not each credential on its own. Rationale: revoke_run_credentials applies a fresh RollbackBudget per token in a sequential loop, so total rollback time grows with the number of providers. No requirement text states the intended scope.

uncertainty.rationale: Single-pass extraction from a codebase with substantial dead and test-only code; reachability judgments were later checked by the adversarial pass.

open_questions: cmd_mint (src/main.rs:725) propagates MintFailed with `?` and never revokes the succeeded tokens, so rollback is live only for `run`. Is mint-mode rollback intended?
The provider subprocess also has its own 30 second ExecConfig timeout in main.rs. Which of the two budgets is the intended limit?
A timeout below one second prints as 0s (test format_timeout_error_sub_second_timeout). Is that acceptable for operators?
The permit is taken in the caller loop before the task spawns, so provider start is serialised behind permit waits. Does the design require true parallel start?
Callers can still build MintConfig through struct literals with max_concurrent 0, because the fields are public. Should the type be sealed?

material_claims.statement: Before a run mode agent process starts its program, noscope puts that process in a new process group that the process itself leads. On Linux noscope also asks the kernel to send SIGTERM to the agent process if noscope dies first. noscope applies neither protection in mint mode.

When noscope forwards a signal to the agent, it sends the signal to the whole agent process group, not to the agent process alone. If the group does not exist, noscope sends the signal to the agent process directly. If neither target exists, noscope treats the forward as done.

The first shutdown signal that noscope receives starts a graceful shutdown. A second SIGTERM or SIGINT during that shutdown makes noscope kill the agent at once and give up on further cleanup. A second SIGHUP does not escalate.
noscope forwards SIGTERM, SIGHUP and SIGINT to the agent process group. noscope does not forward SIGPIPE and does not start a shutdown for SIGPIPE.

noscope acts on a shutdown signal only after the operating system delivers that signal to noscope. noscope never invents a shutdown signal. noscope ignores any delivered signal that is not SIGTERM, SIGINT or SIGHUP.
noscope tries to revoke the minted credentials at most one time during a run. The first shutdown signal starts that revocation. Later shutdown signals do not start a second revocation.

noscope records a signal_received event for every shutdown signal it handles. noscope records a signal_forwarded event only after the forward to the agent succeeds. A failed forward produces no signal_forwarded event.
noscope reports the exit code of the agent process as its own exit code. If a signal killed the agent, noscope reports 128 plus the signal number.

noscope removes every environment variable whose name starts with NOSCOPE_ from the agent environment. noscope refuses to start the agent if a credential asks for an environment name with that prefix.
noscope records a child_spawn event when the agent process starts. noscope records a child_exit event carrying the exit code when the agent process ends.

noscope writes every event as one line with no embedded line break. In the json log format that line is a JSON object. In the text log format it is a readable line that starts with the timestamp and the event type.

Each event carries a timestamp in RFC 3339 form, an event type name in snake case, and a provider name. Each event may also carry a redacted token id, a duration in milliseconds, an exit code, a signal number and an error message.
noscope emits an event for the start, the success and the failure of each mint, refresh and revoke action. noscope also emits events for agent spawn, agent exit, signal receipt and signal forwarding.
noscope accepts only the lowercase words 'json' and 'text' as a log format. Any other value is a usage error and noscope does not start the agent.
noscope writes all events to standard error. noscope never writes an event to standard output. In run mode standard output belongs to the agent alone.
An event never carries a raw credential value. The token id field of an event holds only a redacted identifier.
noscope tries to revoke every minted credential when the agent process ends, whatever the reason for the end. A normal exit, a non-zero exit and a signal death all lead to a revocation attempt.
If noscope cannot start the agent process, noscope revokes the credentials it already minted before it reports the failure.
noscope stays alive until the agent process ends. While it waits, noscope keeps checking for new shutdown signals and forwards each one to the agent.
The run command and the integration runtime must produce the same forwarding and escalation results for the same sequence of shutdown signals.

noscope revokes all active credentials at the same time when a shutdown starts. A failure to revoke one credential does not stop the revocation of the others. noscope reports one result for each credential.

noscope gives credential revocation a wall clock budget of 10 seconds and at most 3 retries. The wait between retries starts at 500 milliseconds and doubles each time. When the budget runs out, noscope stops trying and depends on the token TTL instead.
noscope treats a credential that is already revoked and a credential that has expired as a successful revocation. noscope does not retry either case.
noscope refuses to mint a credential without a TTL. noscope refuses a TTL below 60 seconds. noscope refuses a TTL above 12 hours.

If an operator sets a wall clock limit for the agent process, noscope kills the agent with SIGKILL when the limit passes. noscope then reports 128 plus 9 as the exit code and still revokes the credentials.

In run mode noscope terminates the whole agent process group with SIGTERM. noscope refuses a process group id that is not positive. noscope treats a group that is already gone as terminated. noscope does not terminate groups in mint mode.

In mint mode noscope captures the agent standard output and standard error separately and returns both to the caller. In run mode noscope returns no captured output because the agent writes straight to the terminal.
noscope refuses to start the agent when an injected credential name already exists in the environment, unless the caller asks noscope to override it.
noscope allows the agent a grace period of 30 seconds after the first shutdown signal before it kills the agent with SIGKILL. An operator can change that grace period.
When the agent command does not exist noscope exits with code 127. When the agent command exists but is not executable noscope exits with code 126.

unsupported_recommendations.recommendation: A second SIGTERM or SIGINT cannot actually stop a revocation that is already running, because revocation runs to completion inside the handling of the first signal. Rationale: on_parent_signal calls revoker.revoke_all synchronously and never reads the abandon_revocation field of the decision, so the escalation flag has no effect on cleanup.

A slow provider can make noscope unresponsive to the escalation signal, because the blocking revocation inside the signal handler stops the poll loop from reading the next signal. Rationale: The blocking call chain from on_parent_signal through revoke_on_shutdown_signal to runtime.block_on suggests this, but no test measures responsiveness during revocation.

On a non-Linux Unix target noscope loses process-group termination entirely, so signals reach only the agent process and not its grandchildren. Rationale: configure_child_for_run_mode is a no-op off Linux, so the group kill in forward_signal finds no group and falls back to a single-process kill. No test covers a non-Linux target.

noscope should revoke credentials even when the operating system kills noscope itself with SIGKILL, using the token TTL as the only remaining protection. Rationale: The README lists stronger end-to-end revoke-on-exit guarantees as planned, but no code in this partition addresses the case where noscope cannot run any cleanup.

The process group of the agent should be reaped after the agent leader exits, so that an orphaned grandchild does not keep credentials in use past the run. Rationale: terminate_group_for_mode implements this shape but is not wired to the exit path, and no requirement text in the repository states the obligation.

uncertainty.rationale: Single-pass extraction from a codebase with substantial dead and test-only code; reachability judgments were later checked by the adversarial pass.

material_claims.statement: noscope accepts a provider name or a profile name only when every character is an ASCII letter, digit, hyphen, underscore, or dot. noscope also rejects the empty name and the names '.' and '..'.

noscope refuses to read a provider or profile configuration file when the file is group-writable or grants any permission to other users. Owner-only modes and owner-plus-group-read modes stay allowed.

noscope takes the provider commands from exactly one source. Direct overrides beat environment variables. Environment variables beat the configuration file. noscope never merges values from two sources.
When no override and no configuration file supply a provider, noscope reports the provider as not found and lists every location that it checked.
A provider configuration file must declare contract_version and a commands table that holds a non-empty mint command. noscope rejects any other provider file as malformed.
noscope accepts provider contract version 1 only. noscope rejects every other version and names the supported versions in the error.
A provider that declares support for refresh must also configure a refresh command. A provider that declares support for revoke must also configure a revoke command.
A missing provider configuration file is not an error on its own. noscope treats the file layer as absent and continues with the other sources.
A profile must list at least one credential. Each credential must give a non-empty provider name, a non-empty role, and a whole-number ttl greater than zero.
A profile credential accepts only the fields provider, role, ttl, and env_key. noscope rejects any other field, so a profile cannot inherit, override, or nest another profile.
noscope reports every schema problem in a profile in one error message. noscope does not stop at the first bad credential.
A profile that the user names must exist. noscope reports an error when the named profile file is missing.
A user cannot combine the profile option with the provider, role, or ttl options. noscope rejects such a command line and names the conflicting options.
Before noscope mints from a profile, every provider that the profile names must exist, and every explicit env_key must appear only once.
The validate command reports every configured provider command that is missing or is not executable. The validate command never runs those commands.
The doctor command checks the noscope config directory and every provider TOML file under it. Doctor reports one named check for each item with a pass, warn, or fail status.
The doctor command exits with 78 when any check fails. It exits with 1 when a check warns and none fails. It exits with 0 otherwise.
The doctor command warns, and does not fail, when a provider command is missing or is not executable.
The init command creates the noscope directory and its providers and profiles subdirectories under the config home. init sets each directory it creates to owner-only access, mode 0700.
A second run of the init command does not fail and does not change the permissions of a directory that already exists.
noscope reads provider command overrides from the environment variables NOSCOPE_MINT_CMD, NOSCOPE_REFRESH_CMD, and NOSCOPE_REVOKE_CMD. An empty variable counts as unset.

noscope reads a named provider from the path noscope/providers/<name>.toml under the config home, and a named profile from noscope/profiles/<name>.toml. The config home is XDG_CONFIG_HOME, or the .config directory inside HOME when that variable is unset.
Every noscope path that reads a provider or profile configuration file must check the file permissions before it reads the content.
noscope stops with a configuration error when a provider or profile file is malformed. noscope never mints credentials from a file that it could only partly understand.
The dry-run command shows the mint command, the role, the ttl, and the source layer for a provider. The dry-run command executes nothing.

noscope reports a distinct exit code for each class of configuration failure. A usage error gives 64 and a missing config file gives 66. A permission problem gives 77 and a config error gives 78. A failed profile validation gives 79.
The doctor command only reads. It never creates, changes, or deletes a configuration file or directory.
Each credential in a profile must reach the child process under its own environment variable name. A profile may set that name with env_key.
noscope ignores an unknown top-level key in a profile file so that older versions can read newer profiles. noscope still rejects an unknown key inside a credential entry.
Extra environment variables declared in a provider file reach the provider command only when the configuration file is the winning source.

unsupported_recommendations.recommendation: noscope should reject a resolved provider that has no mint command, whatever layer supplied the configuration. Rationale: resolve_provider_config uses input.mint_cmd.unwrap_or_default() at src/provider.rs:431, so an override layer that sets only a revoke command yields an empty mint command that no check rejects. No test or comment states the intended behaviour.

noscope should redact or omit provider environment values in dry-run output, because a provider file can hold a secret. Rationale: dry_run_output prints every [commands.env] pair verbatim at src/provider.rs:514, and the redaction module is not used there. Nothing in the code or tests states that these values must stay clear.

The doctor command should also check the profiles directory and each profile file for parseability and secure permissions. Rationale: run_init creates the profiles directory but run_doctor inspects only the providers directory. The test named doctor_checks_profiles_dir_existence actually asserts on the providers check, which hints at an unfinished intention.

noscope should verify that a provider or profile config file is owned by the user running noscope. Rationale: check_config_permissions inspects only the mode bits. A file owned by another user with mode 0600 passes. No comment claims ownership is checked.

The provider command string should support arguments and PATH lookup rather than a bare executable path. Rationale: validate_provider and check_command_health both treat the whole command string as a filesystem path, while the README example shows 'aws-mint --role {{role}} --ttl {{ttl}}' with arguments, so the README example would be reported as missing.

Provider and profile config resolution should use one shared config-home computation that every command honours. Rationale: cmd_run and cmd_mint pass XDG_CONFIG_HOME into ClientOptions, cmd_doctor and cmd_init compute it themselves, and cmd_dry_run, cmd_validate, and cmd_revoke ignore it. Nothing states which behaviour is intended.

material_claims.statement: A provider command must return a JSON object that holds a non-empty string field named token. noscope rejects every other output.
When a provider supplies expires_at, noscope accepts only a valid ISO 8601 timestamp. noscope also accepts a timestamp in the past.
When a provider omits expires_at, noscope sets the credential expiry to the current time plus the requested TTL.
noscope accepts a minted credential only when the provider command exits with code 0.
A requested role must contain only ASCII letters, digits, hyphens, underscores and dots. noscope rejects any other role.
noscope must run a provider command as a direct argv execution. noscope must not pass the command to a shell interpreter.
noscope must replace the role placeholder and the TTL placeholder in each provider command argument with the literal requested values.
noscope must give the TTL to a provider command as a plain integer count of seconds with no unit suffix.
noscope must stop a provider command that runs longer than the configured timeout. noscope sends SIGTERM first and SIGKILL after the grace period.
The default provider command timeout is 30 seconds. The default wait after SIGTERM before SIGKILL is 5 seconds.
noscope must report a provider command that timed out as provider exit code 4, which means the provider is unavailable.
noscope must reject provider stdout larger than 1 MiB and must mint no credential from it.
noscope keeps at most 4096 bytes of provider stderr. The cut must not split a UTF-8 character.
Credential values that noscope gives to a provider must not appear in the provider stderr that noscope keeps or shows.
noscope discards provider stderr after a successful provider command unless the user asks for verbose output.
A provider command must start with only PATH, HOME and LANG taken from the parent environment. All other parent variables must stay hidden.
noscope must pass the credential and its identifier to a revoke command through the NOSCOPE_TOKEN and NOSCOPE_TOKEN_ID environment variables.
A revoke command that exits with code 0 counts as success. This includes the case where the credential was already revoked.
noscope must pass NOSCOPE_TOKEN, NOSCOPE_TOKEN_ID and NOSCOPE_TTL to a refresh command. A refresh returns the same JSON contract as a mint.
A provider that declares support for refresh or revoke must also configure the matching command. noscope rejects an inconsistent provider config.
A provider process reports its result by exit code: 0 success, 1 general error, 2 authentication failure, 3 role not found, 4 unavailable.
noscope treats any provider exit code outside 0 to 4 as a general error. A raw code above 128 also reports the signal number, which is the code minus 128.
A provider process killed by a signal must count as a failure and must never yield a credential.
When noscope itself fails, it exits with one fixed sysexits code for the class of failure.
When the child process runs, noscope exits with the exit code of the child without change.
noscope failure codes must never collide with the provider protocol error codes 1 to 4.
Every failure that noscope reports carries one machine-readable category from a closed set: usage, config, provider, security, profile or internal.
Each error category maps to one fixed process exit code: usage 64, config 78, provider 65, security 64, profile 66 and internal 70.
When several providers fail, noscope must report each failure with its own provider name and category instead of one joined string.
Debug or log output of a parsed provider result must never show the raw credential value.
noscope must wipe the raw credential from memory when the parsed provider result goes out of scope.
A provider that writes more output than the pipe buffer holds must still finish. noscope reads stdout and stderr while it waits for exit.
When noscope cannot start the provider executable, it reports a failure and mints no credential.
With JSON output selected, a failed command prints one JSON object with status, command, kind and message fields to stderr.

unsupported_recommendations.recommendation: The intended provider command placeholder syntax is double braces, and the single-brace substitution in the execution engine is a defect that renders a documented config to a literal brace-wrapped value. Rationale: README.md:38 and docs/QUICKSTART.md:28 use {{role}} and {{ttl}}, while substitute_template_vars replaces {role} and {ttl}; no test covers the double-brace form, so which side is authoritative is unresolved.

noscope intends a user-facing refresh workflow that renews a credential before expiry while the child process runs. Rationale: build_refresh_env, refresh.rs RefreshPolicy and the integration harness all exist, but no CLI subcommand reaches them.

The 1 MiB stdout limit is meant to bound noscope memory use against a hostile provider, not only to reject nonsense output. Rationale: The stated intent is not written anywhere, and the current read-then-check order cannot deliver a memory bound.

Provider stderr is meant to be shown to the user on success only under --verbose, and the missing wiring is an unfinished feature rather than a removed one. Rationale: The --verbose help text promises the behavior and StderrPolicy encodes it, but nothing calls the type.

Every provider protocol code from 1 to 4 is meant to drive different noscope behavior, such as retry on 4 and a credential setup hint on 2. Rationale: Only a test in exit_code.rs demonstrates filtering retryable failures; no production path branches on the specific code.

uncertainty.rationale: Single-pass extraction from a codebase with substantial dead and test-only code; reachability judgments were later checked by the adversarial pass.

open_questions: Are unknown extra JSON fields allowed forever, or is a strict schema planned?
Should noscope refuse a credential that is already expired at mint time?
The NS-034 warning is never emitted: main.rs calls provider_output_to_scoped_token, which drops the expires_at_provided flag (src/main.rs:158).
The profile path skips this check: resolve_profile_specs_and_providers (src/main.rs:520) never calls validate_mint, and profile validation only checks that a role is non-empty (src/profile.rs:210).
parse_command falls back to whitespace splitting on unbalanced quotes, which changes the argv a user configured.

The code substitutes single-brace {role} and {ttl}, but README.md:38 and docs/QUICKSTART.md:28 document double-brace {{role}} and {{ttl}}. A config written from the docs renders to a literal brace-wrapped value.
The revoke path (src/main.rs:828) does not substitute placeholders at all.
The signal goes to the child pid only, not to its process group, so provider grandchildren can survive.
Live call sites repeat the numbers instead of using ExecConfig::default, so the default can drift silently.
No CLI flag exposes the timeout to the user.
as_provider_exit_code has no production caller; only execute_provider_command performs the live mapping.
The whole stdout is read into memory before the check, so the limit does not bound memory use.
The check counts characters of the lossy UTF-8 string, not raw bytes.
Truncation keeps the head of stderr, but the useful error is often the last line.
Only values of NOSCOPE_TOKEN-prefixed variables are redacted. Secrets in provider [commands.env] values are not.
Redaction is exact substring matching, so an encoded or split token still leaks.
StderrPolicy is defined but not wired to any live path: no caller exists outside its own tests.
execute_provider_command always returns captured stderr, and no command path prints provider stderr on success, so --verbose does nothing for stderr today.
Provider config env plus NOSCOPE_* values are merged on top, so the effective set is larger than three.
When PATH, HOME or LANG are unset, fixed fallbacks /usr/bin:/bin, /root and C.UTF-8 are used.
The live revoke path passes an empty NOSCOPE_TOKEN because only the token id is known (src/main.rs:836), so the value half of this rule is unmet in the CLI.
Nothing tells a provider author how to signal already-revoked apart from exit 0.
No refresh subcommand exists in the CLI (src/cli.rs:85), and integration_runtime.rs is only used by tests/integration_test_suite.rs, so this path is not user-reachable.
The provider_exec wrappers validate_capabilities and parse_capabilities_from_toml have no production caller; enforcement, if any, lives in src/provider.rs.
Nothing in the live command paths reacts differently to code 2, 3 or 4; they all become a mint failure string.
Negative codes map to a general error with no signal, which only matters on non-Unix platforms.
On Unix a signal death gives no exit code, so the signal number is lost and the 128-plus-signal branch only fires for shell-reported codes.
Codes 69 unavailable and 77 permission have no reachable producer through error.rs; only profile.rs and mint.rs use some of them.
Exit code 0 from a child cannot be told apart from noscope's own success at the process level.
A child process may still exit with 1 to 4 and be indistinguishable from a provider protocol code.
Every From conversion collapses the source error into a formatted string message, so the sub-detail stays stringly.
A security violation and a usage error share code 64, so a caller cannot tell them apart by exit code alone.
MultiProviderReport is defined but not wired to any live path; only its own tests use it.
Error::multi has no production caller.
The live multi-provider mint failure returns Error::config, so it exits 78 and not the intended 65.
ProviderExecResult.stdout is a plain String that still holds the raw JSON token, and its derived Debug prints it.
The same token also exists in ProviderExecResult.stdout and in the environment map, and neither is zeroized.
Inner errors of a multi-error never appear in the JSON object, because only message and kind are printed.

material_claims.statement: A mint operation over several providers must succeed for all providers or produce no credentials at all. On any provider failure the system must revoke every credential that it already minted.
The system must reject a credential set in which two credentials ask for the same environment variable name. The error must name every conflicting provider.
Each provider mint attempt must have its own time limit. The default limit must be 30 seconds and an operator must be able to change it.
The rollback of already minted credentials must run under a shared wall-clock budget. The system must retry revocation with growing backoff and must stop when the budget ends.
Every rollback attempt must be written to the log. Each log entry must carry the credential identifier and the credential time to live.
The system must compute a refresh time for each credential from that credential expiry time alone. The system must not batch credentials into one shared refresh schedule.
When a credential expires while the child process runs, the system must only log a warning. The system must not kill the child process and must not mint a replacement.
The system must limit how many provider mint commands run at the same time. The default limit must be 8 and a limit of 0 must be rejected.

Provider configuration must resolve from exactly one source layer. Command line flags beat environment variables and environment variables beat configuration files. The system must not merge values across layers.
An environment variable that holds an empty string must not activate the environment layer of provider configuration.
Provider configuration files must live under the XDG config directory in a noscope providers folder. When the XDG variable is unset the system must fall back to the home config directory.
A provider configuration file that the system cannot parse must cause a hard error. A configuration file that does not exist must not cause an error because that layer is simply absent.
When no layer supplies a provider configuration, the error must list every location that the system checked. The list must include the flag name, the environment variable name, and the file path.
The system must refuse to read a secret-bearing configuration file when the file is group-writable or readable by others. Modes such as 0600 and 0640 must stay acceptable.
The same permission check must apply to provider configuration files and to profile configuration files.

A dry run must show the resolved provider, the config source, and the mint, refresh, and revoke commands. It must also show the role, the time to live, and the environment variables. A dry run must not execute any provider command.
The validate command must check that every configured provider command exists on disk and carries execute permission. The validate command must not run those commands.
When validation fails, the error must name the failing command type and the concrete command path.
A provider mint command must print JSON that contains a non-empty string token. The command may also print an ISO 8601 expiry time.

When the provider does not report an expiry time, the system must set the expiry to the current time plus the requested time to live. The system must also record that the provider did not supply the expiry so a warning can follow.

The system must substitute the role and the time to live into the provider argument list without a shell. The system must reject a role that contains anything other than letters, digits, hyphens, underscores, and dots.
The system must write the time to live into provider arguments as an integer number of seconds. The system must not use human duration suffixes.
A provider command that runs too long must first receive SIGTERM and then SIGKILL after a grace period. The default limit must be 30 seconds and the default grace period must be 5 seconds.
The system must reject provider output that is larger than 1 mebibyte.
A revoke command must receive the token and the token identifier through the environment. A revoke command must not receive a time to live.
A revoke command that exits with status 0 must count as success. A token that was already revoked or already expired must therefore count as revoked.
A refresh command must receive the token, the token identifier, and the time to live in seconds. Refresh output must follow the same JSON contract as mint output.
The system must truncate captured provider error output to 4096 bytes at a safe character boundary. The system must replace any known token value in that output with a redaction marker.
A provider must declare whether it supports refresh and whether it supports revoke. The system must reject a declaration of support when the matching command is missing.

A provider subprocess must start with a minimal environment that contains only the path, home, and language variables plus the variables that noscope injects. No other variable of the parent process may reach the provider.
A provider configuration file must declare a contract version. The system must accept only the current version and the version before it.
The mint output must be a JSON envelope that carries the token, the expiry time, the token identifier, the provider, and the role.
The mint command must print a JSON array that holds one envelope for every requested provider. The command must print nothing when any provider fails.
The mint envelope on standard output is the one place where the raw token appears. Log output and debug output must show a redacted form instead.
The mint command must refuse to write a token when standard output is a terminal. The command must exit with code 64 and must tell the operator about the scrollback risk and the override flag.
The mint command must require a non-zero time to live, at least one provider, and a non-empty role.
The revoke command must accept either a token identifier together with a provider name or a mint envelope on standard input. Both forms must reach the provider through one shared input path.
The system must never accept a raw token value on the command line. The system must reject a revoke invocation that carries a token flag in any form.
The system reads a mint envelope from standard input for revocation. The system must discard the raw token value from that envelope. The system must keep only the token identifier and the provider.
A refresh failure must never kill the child process. The system must retry with backoff while retries remain and then allow the credential to expire, and it must always log a warning.
Refresh retries must start at 1 second, double each attempt, stop after 4 retries, and vary by up to 25 percent. The whole retry window must stay within half of the remaining credential lifetime.
Each credential must track its own refresh failures. A failure on one credential must not change the retry state of another credential.
A run of failures must never disable refresh for good. The system must try to refresh again at the next normal interval.
When the system starts in rotate mode it must warn the operator that credentials in environment variables are point-in-time values.
In run mode the child process must start in its own process group. The child must receive SIGTERM if the noscope parent process dies.
When the run ends, the system must terminate the whole child process group. The system must refuse a process group identifier that is zero or negative.
Process group creation and parent-death signalling must apply in run mode only. Mint mode must not change process group behaviour.
The system must forward SIGTERM, SIGINT, and SIGHUP from the parent to the child process. The system must ignore SIGPIPE.
The system must only forward a shutdown signal after the operating system actually delivers one. The system must never create a shutdown signal by itself.
A second shutdown signal must escalate to an immediate SIGKILL of the child. One signal alone must not escalate.
The first shutdown signal must start revocation of every minted credential. Revocation must not start before a shutdown signal arrives.
Revocation of several credentials must run in parallel. A failure for one credential must not stop revocation of the others, and each credential must get its own retry budget.
The revocation retry budget must default to 10 seconds of wall clock time, 500 milliseconds of base backoff, and 3 retries. A budget of zero must disable retries.
A requested time to live must be at least 60 seconds and at most 12 hours by default. The mint path must reject a missing, too short, or too long time to live.
The run command must mint every credential before it starts the child process. The command must inject the minted credentials into the child environment.
The run command must exit with the exact exit code of the child process.
The run command must revoke every minted credential after the child ends. The command must also revoke them when the child fails to start.

The system must emit a structured event for every mint, refresh, and revoke attempt and for its result. The system must also emit events for child start, child exit, signal receipt, and signal forwarding.
Events must go to the error stream, not to the standard output stream. Each event must be one line of JSON when the operator selects the JSON log format.
An event must never carry a raw token value. Only a redacted token identifier supplied by the caller may appear in an event.
Every success message must go to the standard output stream. A successful command must write nothing to the error stream.
In JSON output mode a successful command must write one JSON object to standard output. The object must report an ok status, the command name, and the provider.

In JSON output mode a failing command must write one JSON object to the error stream and nothing to standard output. The object must report an error status, the error kind, the command name, and a message.
The failure message that reaches the operator must include the text that the provider command wrote to its error stream.
The doctor command must check that the configuration directory exists and can be read.
The doctor command must check every provider configuration file. The check must confirm that the file parses and that its permissions are secure.
The doctor command must check that each configured provider command exists and carries execute permission.
The doctor command must always produce a report. Each check in the report must carry a name, a pass, warn, or fail status, and a message.
The doctor exit code must show the worst check status. All checks passing must give 0, warnings only must give 1, and any failure must give 78.
A provider command that is not installed must count as a warning. A configuration file that is malformed or has insecure permissions must count as a failure.
The init command must create the noscope configuration directory and its providers and profiles subdirectories under the XDG config directory.
The init command must create every directory with owner-only permissions, mode 0700.
Running the init command a second time must not fail and must not change the permissions of directories that already exist.

The system must reject a provider name or a profile name that is not a safe file name component. Only letters, digits, hyphens, underscores, and dots are allowed, and empty, single dot, and double dot names are rejected.
A name that tries to escape the configuration directory must be reported as a security failure, not as a configuration failure.
The public interface must return errors that carry a machine-readable category. The categories are usage, config, provider, security, profile, and internal.
The process exit code must follow the error category. Usage and security must give 64, config must give 78, provider must give 65, profile must give 66, and internal must give 70.
An error that gathers several failures must keep each failure with its own category and provider name. The system must not flatten them into one string.
The system must fail to start when it cannot disable core dumps. The caller must receive that failure instead of a silent success.
The system must copy a secret only through one conversion path from provider output to scoped token to mint envelope. Every copy must be wiped from memory when it goes out of use.
A type that holds a secret must not be copyable and must not be serialisable. Its debug output must show a redacted value.
The system must refuse a run that names a profile together with direct credential flags.
A profile must let the operator name several credentials. Each credential must carry a provider, a role, a time to live, and an optional environment variable name.
When a profile credential does not name an environment variable, the system must generate a name from the provider name.
The system must pass the provider name and the role to the mint command through the environment.
The system must split a configured command string into arguments and must keep a quoted segment as one argument.
A provider whose configuration names an empty mint command must produce an error before any process starts.
The user documentation must show the placeholder syntax that the system really substitutes into provider commands.
The documentation must tell the operator which safety behaviours work today and which ones are still planned.
The system rests on three safety layers: process-group termination, revocation at exit, and expiry by time to live. Only expiry by time to live is fully guaranteed today.
A scoped token must always carry an expiry time.
The system must keep token material out of process arguments and out of default log output.
All command workflows must reach the same core operations through one shared entry point.

unsupported_recommendations.recommendation: The Cargo manifest must declare the 2021 Rust edition. Rationale: Process artifact. tests/noscope_3ed_edition.rs line 10 asserts a string in Cargo.toml and .beads/provenance-drafts/noscope-3ed.md line 8 writes it as a rule, but it describes the build setup, not system behaviour.

The README must contain an Install heading, the phrase Safety Layers, and the provider config example strings. Rationale: Process artifact. tests/noscope_3ez_7_docs.rs lines 20 to 47 assert literal substrings in documentation files. The underlying intent, that a first-time user can install and configure the tool, is captured as a real candidate instead.

The QUICKSTART document must mention the dry-run, mint, revoke, and run commands. Rationale: Process artifact. tests/noscope_3ez_7_docs.rs line 58 checks for command name substrings. It documents the command surface but tests the file, not the system.

Command line parsing types must live in an adapter module and must stay out of the core library. Rationale: Architecture constraint from .beads/provenance-drafts/noscope-9l0.md line 35 and noscope-cg8.2.md line 22. It describes code structure and does not survive a rewrite as an observable obligation.

Test-only helper modules must not be public in release builds, and unit tests must sit beside the module they exercise. Rationale: Process artifact from .beads/provenance-drafts/noscope-s9i.md lines 10 to 13. It governs the repository layout, not the running system.

The run-mode signal loop and the integration signal loop must produce the same forwarding and escalation outcomes for the same signal sequence. Rationale: From .beads/provenance-drafts/noscope-3ez.3.md line 15. This is a parity obligation between the binary and the test-only shadow runtime in src/integration_runtime.rs. It is a testing strategy, not a product requirement, and it is fragile: the shadow runtime is known to skip template substitution.

The revoke command must pass the real token value to the provider revoke command. Rationale: src/integration_runtime.rs line 129 passes token.expose_secret() to build_revoke_env, but the binary revoke path is reported to pass an empty string. No artifact in this partition states which behaviour is correct. A provider that needs the token value to revoke would work under the shadow runtime and fail under the binary.

The system must warn the operator when a provider does not report an expiry time. Rationale: .beads/provenance-drafts/noscope-ydn.md line 13 and noscope-cg8.3.md line 13 say a flag is preserved so the caller can emit a warning, but no artifact in this partition shows the warning being emitted.

The doctor command and the init command must support both text and JSON output. Rationale: .beads/provenance-drafts/noscope-3ez.12.md line 29 states both commands accept --output text or json, but no test in this partition exercises doctor or init through the binary.

The NS numbering scheme must assign one meaning to each identifier. Rationale: NS-080 and NS-081 each carry two unrelated meanings: doctor checks in src/doctor.rs and the noscope-3ez.12 draft, and CLI output-mode contracts in tests/cli_output_contract.rs. NS-079 appears only in that test file and has no written definition anywhere. This is a bookkeeping defect, not a system requirement.

The system must emit shell completions for bash, zsh, and fish. Rationale: .beads/provenance-drafts/noscope-9l0.md line 18 mentions completion generation for three shells, but no test or document in this partition states it as an obligation or checks it.

material_claims.statement: noscope must not write a credential value to disk or to any persistent store. A credential exists only in process memory and on the mint stdout stream.
Every credential that noscope holds in memory must carry an expiry time. The system must not create a credential without an expiry.
A redacted credential must not keep the raw credential value. The redacted form must be computed once and the raw value must be dropped.
Redaction must hide a JWT completely and must hide any credential of 16 bytes or less completely. For a longer credential noscope may show the first 8 characters followed by three dots.
When noscope identifies a credential without a provider identifier it must derive a stable identifier from the credential itself, and the same credential must always give the same identifier.
Any log line, error message, diagnostic dump or stderr message that mentions a credential must show only the redacted form. No log level, environment variable or command flag may turn redaction off.
The mint command stdout is the single channel that may carry a raw credential. Every other output channel must stay redacted.

The mint command must refuse to print credentials when stdout is a terminal, because the credential would stay in scrollback. The user must be able to override the refusal with an explicit flag. The refusal must exit with the usage exit code 64.
The mint command must reject a request that has no TTL, no provider, or an empty role. The TTL must be at least 60 seconds and at most 12 hours.
The mint command must emit credentials for all requested providers or none. Partial output must never reach stdout.

The mint command must output one JSON array on a single line. Each element must carry exactly five items: the credential, the expiry in RFC 3339 form, the credential identifier, the provider name and the role.
Revocation must work from the credential identifier and the provider name alone. noscope must not require or keep the credential value in order to revoke it.
noscope must accept a mint envelope on standard input for revocation, and must reject an envelope that lacks the credential identifier or the provider name.
noscope must reject a command line that carries a raw credential as an argument. An opaque credential identifier stays allowed as an argument.
A credential must reach a child process or a provider command only through an environment variable. noscope must never place a credential in a command argument.
noscope must disable core dumps for its own process before it loads any credential, and must set both the soft and the hard limit to zero.
noscope must erase credential material from memory as soon as the owner of that material goes away, and must not let a credential be copied without a known owner for each copy.
When noscope turns provider output into an in-memory credential it must attach the role, the provider name and a credential identifier, and must keep the expiry that came out of the provider step.
When a provider does not return an expiry, noscope must compute one from the requested TTL and must warn the user that the expiry is not authoritative.
When noscope abandons a mint request before it finishes, it must run a cleanup step, because the provider may already have created a credential.
A provider must offer mint, refresh and revoke for a credential. A refresh must return a new credential and must leave the old credential unchanged.
An error or diagnostic message about a credential must name only a location or an opaque identifier. It must never contain the credential itself.
Every minted credential must carry an identifier that lets the user revoke it later without holding the credential value.

unsupported_recommendations.recommendation: The pre-computed redacted string of a long credential leaves the first 8 characters of that credential in memory after the credential is zeroized. Rationale: ScopedToken::drop zeroizes the role and the metadata but not the RedactedToken it holds, and for a value over 16 bytes that string holds a real prefix. Whether this counts as a breach of the zeroization obligation is a judgement the code does not record.

Showing the first 8 characters of a long credential is itself a partial disclosure and may be the wrong default for a credential manager. Rationale: The code argues the opposite way for the byte-length threshold, choosing the fully opaque branch when in doubt, so the prefix branch looks like a legacy debugging convenience rather than a considered rule.

The documented pipeline `noscope mint | noscope revoke --from-stdin` cannot work, because mint always emits a JSON array and from_mint_json parses only a single object. Rationale: README.md line 75 shows the pipe, format_mint_output always returns an array, and from_mint_json calls get("token_id") on the parsed value. I did not run the commands to confirm the failure.

The TokenProvider trait, CleanupOnDropFuture and validate_no_tokens_in_args are the remains of an earlier design in which a provider was a Rust object rather than an external command. Rationale: All three are complete, tested and unreachable, while the live code reaches providers by spawning commands. I found no design note that states this history.

A provider that needs the credential value to revoke it cannot be used through the noscope revoke command. Rationale: execute_revoke passes an empty NOSCOPE_TOKEN, while the run-mode revoke path passes the real value. Whether any real provider needs the value is outside what the code shows.

contributions.strongest_finding: The supervisor rule named the wrong symbol: forwarding, once-only revoke and escalation live in RunSignalWiring::on_parent_signal, and the once-only test bypasses the supervisor loop entirely.

challenges.objection: [narrow-the-statement] The phrase 'every configured provider command' reads as all providers, but cmd_validate (src/main.rs:888-891) resolves exactly one provider and validate_provider checks only that provider's mint, refresh, and revoke strings. The statement also hides the mechanism that decides 'missing': check_command_executable (src/provider.rs:550-556) calls Path::new(cmd) on the whole command string, so it performs no shlex split and no PATH lookup. A command with arguments or a bare binary name on PATH is reported as not found even though it would run.

[demote-rule-to-requirement] The named symbol cannot realize the obligation. dry_run_output (src/provider.rs:493-522) is a pure String formatter and can prove nothing about execution. The no-execution guarantee lives in cmd_dry_run (src/main.rs:1099-1128), which simply never calls provider_exec. Worse for the rule shape, dry_run_output serves only the text branch. The JSON branch at src/main.rs:1107-1125 builds its own serde_json object and never calls dry_run_output, so the named symbol covers half the command. The statement also omits a disclosed field: both branches print the provider [commands.env] map verbatim, at src/provider.rs:514-519 and src/main.rs:1122.

[narrow-the-statement] The statement overstates coverage on three counts. First, 'every provider file under it' is wrong: check_providers (src/doctor.rs:159-177) reads only the direct entries of noscope/providers and skips every file whose extension is not toml, with no recursion. Second, the claim describes unconditional coverage, but run_doctor returns after a single check when the noscope directory is missing (src/doctor.rs:136), and it emits only a warning and checks nothing further when the providers directory is missing (src/doctor.rs:141-149). Third, the candidate bundles three separate obligations into one rule keyed to run_doctor: what gets checked, the shape of a check result, and the infallibility of the command. The shape obligation is realized by the Check and DoctorReport types (src/doctor.rs:38-52), and the check pushes are spread across run_doctor, check_providers, and check_command_health.

[narrow-the-statement] The failure half is imprecise in a way that matters. 'Insecure permissions count as a failure' names no subject, and doctor only inspects the permissions of the provider TOML file, through provider::check_config_permissions at src/doctor.rs:187-194. Doctor never inspects the permissions of any directory, so the 0700 mode that init deliberately sets on noscope, providers, and profiles (src/doctor.rs:325) is never verified by doctor. An operator who loosens those directories to 0777 gets a clean doctor report.

[narrow-the-statement] Two objections. First, no enforcement path exists. I read every call in run_doctor, check_providers, and check_command_health (src/doctor.rs:115-295) and confirmed they are all reads: is_dir, read_dir, read_to_string, metadata, and Path::exists. That makes the claim true today, but it is an absence property with no type, no test, and no guard preventing a future check from writing. Second, the third sentence is a different obligation. 'A missing directory produces a failing check that points at init' is a message-content claim about src/doctor.rs:127-134 and duplicates the missing-directory behaviour already carried by backtrace/doctor/checks.

[narrow-the-statement] 'Every directory it creates gets owner-only permissions' is false as written, and the gap is a security gap. run_init calls fs::create_dir_all(dir) at src/doctor.rs:323 and only then calls fs::set_permissions on that same dir at line 325. Two consequences follow. First, create_dir_all creates any missing parents, for example XDG_CONFIG_HOME itself, and those parents are never passed to set_permissions, so they keep the umask mode. Second, even the three named directories exist at the umask mode, typically 0755, for the window between the create call and the chmod call, so init never creates a directory at 0700 atomically.

[narrow-the-statement] The third sentence does not belong to the named symbol. run_init returns an InitResult carrying created_dirs (src/doctor.rs:329-331) and reports nothing. The 'nothing to do' message is produced by cmd_init at src/main.rs:1217-1218 when created_dirs is empty. Keying a rule to run_init while the statement asserts operator-visible output makes the rule unfalsifiable against its own symbol.

[narrow-the-statement] The statement merges two obligations into one sentence. The injection half duplicates backtrace/run/child-env-injection, which covers the same code at src/main.rs:202-206 and 362. Stripping it leaves the ordering obligation, which is the real content. The statement also omits the consequence that gives the ordering its point: on any mint failure cmd_run returns an error at src/main.rs:195-197, before line 209 ever spawns the child, so a failed mint means no child process at all.

[narrow-the-statement] The word 'only' is an unenforced absence claim. Nothing in the codebase prevents a credential from reaching the child by another channel, and no test asserts the absence. It is true at this commit because cmd_run passes credentials solely through the env HashMap built at src/main.rs:202-206, but that is inspection, not enforcement. The override half is genuinely enforced and should be stated with its cost: force_env is hardcoded true at src/main.rs:363, so the EnvCollision branch at src/agent_process.rs:105-107 can never fire in production and the overwrite happens silently with no warning and no opt-out flag.

[narrow-the-statement] The statement is unconditional but the naming rule has an exception it does not mention. A profile may set an explicit env_key per credential, read at src/main.rs:538-539 in resolve_profile_specs_and_providers, and CredentialSet::env_map (src/credential_set.rs:300-305) keys purely off spec.env_key. So the derived name applies to the flag path only. The statement also asserts the mapping without noting that nothing validates the provider name first.

[narrow-the-statement] The naming half does not hold everywhere. The mint and revoke call sites do name the provider and the command type, but the refresh path does not. src/integration_runtime.rs:190 parses the refresh command and passes argv straight to execute_provider_command with no call-site guard, so an empty refresh command produces the generic io error 'argv must not be empty' with no provider name and no command type. The statement also misplaces the enforcement. The never-run guarantee is not carried by the three cited call-site guards at all. It is enforced centrally by execute_provider_command at src/provider_exec.rs:462-467, which rejects an empty argv before it constructs a Command. The call-site guards are message-quality wrappers over that backstop, not the enforcement.

[narrow-the-statement] The named symbol realizes only part of the obligation. exit_status_code (src/agent_process.rs:289-303) is a private free function that maps an ExitStatus to an integer. The claim 'the run command exits with the exact exit code of the child' additionally requires try_wait_exit_code at src/agent_process.rs:187-206, the return at src/main.rs:404, the return at src/main.rs:214, and the unchecked ExitCode::from(code as u8) cast at src/main.rs:39.
