[narrow-the-statement] The second half of the statement, "so substituted values stay inert", does not hold. noscope never invokes a shell itself, but nothing stops an operator from making the shell the provider command. The test fixtures and the wiring tests do exactly that, for example tests/cmd_mint_wiring.rs:150 sets the mint command to /bin/sh -c with the placeholders inside the shell script. In that shape substitute_template_vars writes the role straight into a shell program. Role characters are filtered by validate_role, but only on the flag path through client.validate_mint at src/main.rs:503 and src/main.rs:636. The profile path at src/main.rs:520 never validates the role, so a profile role reaches the command unchecked. A second gap sits in parse_command (src/command_parse.rs:9). When shlex fails on unbalanced quotes the function silently falls back to whitespace splitting and builds a different argv rather than reporting an error.

[narrow-the-statement] The statement says "each provider command argument" without saying which command. Only the mint command is substituted. The two live call sites are src/main.rs:143 and src/main.rs:686, both inside the mint closure. The revoke path at src/main.rs:828 calls parse_command and then executes the argv directly, so {role} and {ttl} in a revoke command reach the provider as literal text. The contested note about the documentation is also imprecise. Because replace scans for the substring {role}, the documented form {{role}} becomes the role wrapped in single braces, for example {admin}, not the untouched text {{role}}.

[narrow-the-statement] As written the statement asserts a fact that is false today, so it reads as a finding rather than a requirement. The documentation at README.md:38, README.md:48 and docs/QUICKSTART.md:28 all show {{role}} and {{ttl}}, while src/provider_exec.rs:263 substitutes {role} and {ttl}. The consequence stated in the contested note is also wrong in detail. A configuration copied from the documentation does not send the literal text {{role}}. The inner substring matches, so the provider receives the role wrapped in braces, for example --role {admin} --ttl {3600}.

[demote-rule-to-requirement] The named symbol does not carry the whole obligation. execute_provider_command holds the escalation logic at src/provider_exec.rs:521-547, but it does not hold the limits. ExecConfig::default at src/provider_exec.rs:132 has no production caller at all. The three live call sites each build an ExecConfig literal with 30 seconds and 5 seconds by hand, at src/main.rs:148, src/main.rs:691 and src/main.rs:844. The numbers are therefore a duplicated constant across four places and can drift. Two behavioral objections also stand. First, send_signal at src/provider_exec.rs:607 calls libc::kill on the child pid alone, never on the process group, so any process the provider started survives the escalation. The process group helper in src/process_group.rs is wired only to the run-mode agent child at src/agent_process.rs:122, never to provider execution. Second, the limit does not bound the call. After the child is reaped the function awaits the two drain tasks at src/provider_exec.rs:550-551 with no time limit, so a surviving grandchild that still holds the standard output pipe blocks the function forever. For mint and run the separate orchestrator timeout at src/orchestrator.rs:70 hides this, but the revoke path at src/main.rs:841 has no outer bound.

[narrow-the-statement] The mapping is live but almost unobservable. src/provider_exec.rs:563-565 sets exit_result to interpret_provider_exit(4) on timeout, yet the mint paths never read exit_result. src/main.rs:171 and src/main.rs:714 report parsed_output, whose Timeout variant renders as "provider command timed out after 30s" with no mention of code 4. Only execute_revoke reads the label, at src/main.rs:857. The label also does not propagate to noscope's own exit status, so a timed-out mint does not produce exit 69 for Unavailable. The contested note is correct and verified: ProviderExecError::as_provider_exit_code at src/provider_exec.rs:85 has one caller and it is the test at src/provider_exec.rs:914.

[narrow-the-statement] The first contested note is correct and matters. src/provider_exec.rs:503-510 reads the whole standard output with read_to_end before any check runs, so the limit is an output-contract check and not a memory guard. A hostile provider can still exhaust memory. The second contested note is wrong. src/provider_exec.rs:577 passes stdout.len(), and Rust String::len returns bytes, not characters. The measured value is the byte length after the lossy UTF-8 conversion at src/provider_exec.rs:553, which can only grow relative to the raw bytes, so the check is conservative and never permissive. The statement also hides the boundary: src/provider_exec.rs:273 compares with a strict greater-than, so output of exactly 1 mebibyte passes, as the test at src/provider_exec.rs:937 asserts. Finally the named symbol is a pure predicate. The refusal to mint is realized by src/provider_exec.rs:577, which turns the Err into parsed_output, so keep both sites.

[narrow-the-statement] The statement promises a guarantee that the shipped code does not deliver. src/provider_exec.rs:476-480 collects redaction candidates only from extra_env entries whose key starts with NOSCOPE_TOKEN. On both live mint paths extra_env holds the provider configuration env plus NOSCOPE_PROVIDER and NOSCOPE_ROLE, and no NOSCOPE_TOKEN key at all, see src/main.rs:139-141 and src/main.rs:682-684. On the live revoke path src/main.rs:836 calls build_revoke_env with an empty token string, and redact_stderr skips empty needles at src/provider_exec.rs:345, so only the credential identifier is ever replaced. No live command passes a credential value to a provider today, so the redaction pass removes nothing in production. Worse, the credential that the provider just printed on standard output is never added to the candidate list, so a provider that echoes its own token to standard error leaks it into captured stderr and into revoke error text. The truncate-before-redact order at src/provider_exec.rs:557-559 adds a third hole for a token that straddles byte 4096. Keep the claim as unsupported in its guarantee form.

[reclassify-as-speculation] No code realizes this statement. StderrPolicy at src/provider_exec.rs:148 has three callers and all three are unit tests at src/provider_exec.rs:1173, :1182 and :1191. The verbose flag reaches ClientOptions.verbose at src/client.rs:49 by way of src/main.rs:98 and src/main.rs:616, and that field is never read anywhere outside its own definition, default and tests. No command prints provider standard error on success. execute_provider_command captures stderr unconditionally and both mint call sites discard the ProviderExecResult when parsing succeeds. The only surviving artifact is the promise in the --verbose help text at src/cli.rs:57. Keep the claim as exploratory and unsupported.

[demote-rule-to-requirement] The named symbol builds the base but does not create the guarantee. build_sandboxed_env at src/provider_exec.rs:396 only returns a three-entry map. The exclusion of every other parent variable comes from cmd.env_clear() at src/provider_exec.rs:487. Remove that one line and the map becomes additive and the whole parent environment leaks, while build_sandboxed_env stays unchanged. Two sites share the obligation, so the rule shape does not hold. The statement is also imprecise about what else reaches the provider. Beyond the variables noscope injects, the provider configuration supplies its own [commands.env] table, parsed at src/provider.rs:304 and merged at src/main.rs:139 and src/main.rs:682, and those values are operator supplied rather than system injected.

[reclassify-as-speculation] No user can reach this contract, so it is not a requirement backtraced from observable behavior. The Command enum at src/cli.rs:85 lists Run, Mint, Revoke, Validate, DryRun, Doctor, Init and Completions, and there is no Refresh. build_refresh_env at src/provider_exec.rs:311 has exactly one non-test caller, src/integration_runtime.rs:192, and that module is exercised only by src/event_emission_wiring_tests.rs and tests/integration_test_suite.rs. The refresh policy module src/refresh.rs is reachable only from the same shadow runtime. The second sentence, that refresh output follows the mint JSON contract, is true only because the shadow runtime routes refresh through the same execute_provider_command call. Keep the claim as exploratory and unsupported.

[demote-rule-to-requirement] A type does not enforce a protocol. ProviderExitCode at src/exit_code.rs:14 is a vocabulary, and nothing rejects a provider that uses a code outside the set. The obligation is spread over the enum, the from_raw table at src/exit_code.rs:41, the interpretation at src/exit_code.rs:184, the live mapping at src/provider_exec.rs:565-567 and the one consumer that acts on a raw value, src/main.rs:857. The contested note is nearly right and needs one correction. No live path branches differently on 2, 3 or 4, but the distinction is not invisible: src/provider_exec.rs:584-589 embeds both the raw code and the Display text in the mint failure message, so an operator does read "provider exit 2: auth failure" rather than a single generic string.

[narrow-the-statement] The mapping inside interpret_provider_exit is stated correctly, but the sentence says "the system" and therefore claims an end-to-end behavior that does not occur. A process that a signal really killed reports no exit code at all. src/provider_exec.rs:562 calls exit_status.code().unwrap_or(1), so the value that reaches interpret_provider_exit is 1 and the greater-than-128 branch never fires. That branch fires only when an intermediate shell propagates 128 plus the signal number as its own exit code. The statement should also record the exact boundary, because 128 itself takes the plain general-error path, as the test at src/exit_code.rs:559 asserts.

[narrow-the-statement] The claim that a noisy provider "still finishes" holds only for a provider that leaves no children behind. The drain tasks are spawned at src/provider_exec.rs:503-519, but they are awaited at src/provider_exec.rs:550-551 after the child is reaped, and those awaits carry no time limit. Because send_signal at src/provider_exec.rs:607 targets the child pid alone, a grandchild that inherited the standard output pipe keeps it open and read_to_end never returns. The function then blocks past its own timeout. For mint and run the orchestrator timeout at src/orchestrator.rs:70 cancels the task, but the revoke call at src/main.rs:841 has no outer bound.

unsupported_recommendations.recommendation: The intended behavior is that the system discards provider standard error after a success unless the operator passes --verbose. The system always keeps standard error after a failure. The code does not implement the success half of this behavior. StderrPolicy has no production caller and the verbose flag never reaches a stderr decision.

The intended refresh contract gives the provider the credential, the credential identifier and the TTL in seconds through environment variables. Refresh output is meant to follow the same JSON contract as mint output. No refresh subcommand exists, so no operator can reach this contract. Only the shadow integration runtime calls the environment builder.

uncertainty.rationale: Every verdict was formed by reading the cited sites at the pinned commit; several were confirmed by running the pinned binary.

contributions.strongest_finding: The half-lifetime retry bound is unenforced and untestable: it is checked per attempt and max_retry_window clamps its own return so the bound test can never fail.

challenges.objection: [narrow-the-statement] The second sentence is not enforced. on_refresh_failure at src/refresh.rs:163 compares a single attempt delay against half of the remaining lifetime, never the cumulative window, and it re-reads the lifetime remaining at that moment rather than spending a fixed budget. max_retry_window at src/refresh.rs:103-115 ends with total_ms.min(half_remaining_ms), so it clamps its own answer and can never report a breach. The test at src/refresh.rs:750 asserts max_window <= half_remaining, which that clamp guarantees unconditionally, so the stated bound has no test behind it. Confirmed by reading src/refresh.rs:103 as instructed.

[narrow-the-statement] The runtime never resets the retry budget. reset_retry_window at src/refresh.rs:524 and should_attempt_refresh at src/refresh.rs:518 have no production caller, only tests at src/refresh.rs:875 and src/refresh.rs:914. record_refresh_failure clears consecutive_failures only through a success. After 4 failures every later failure returns AllowExpiry immediately, so the fresh set of retries that the NS-032 draft promises never arrives. The cluster cites src/refresh.rs:518 as evidence for a function that nothing calls.

[narrow-the-statement] The expiry claim fails on the only path that reaches a provider. build_refresh_env at src/provider_exec.rs:311 sets NOSCOPE_TOKEN, NOSCOPE_TOKEN_ID and NOSCOPE_TTL, and NOSCOPE_TTL is a lifetime in whole seconds rather than an expiry instant. Nothing converts a RefreshExecutionRequest into a provider invocation, so the expires_at field at src/refresh.rs:255 reaches no provider at all. token_id is also optional at src/refresh.rs:253, so the identifier can be absent.

[reclassify-as-speculation] No stated obligation backs this classification. No NS rule in .beads/provenance-drafts mentions leases, renewal or rotation, unlike every other refresh cluster that cites an NS number. Nothing reads LeaseRefreshKind either. run_once returns it inside RuntimeRefreshEvent at src/refresh.rs:262 and every caller drops the value. NS-025 already states that the child never sees a refreshed credential, so the distinction changes nothing an operator can act on. The second sentence about clearing the failure count duplicates the per-credential-isolation cluster and states a tracker mechanic rather than an obligation.

[demote-to-detail] This restates how any timer works and adds no obligation beyond the 75 percent schedule rule and per-credential independence. next_wake_delay at src/refresh.rs:303 only returns the smallest remaining delay and it never sleeps. No production code calls it and no NS rule asks for it, so the phrase about the runtime sleeping describes a caller that does not exist. The stated purpose, that no credential misses its own refresh time, follows from per-credential scheduling and is not an independent constraint.

[narrow-the-statement] compute_refresh_at at src/credential_set.rs:419 takes 75 percent of the time remaining at the moment of the call, not 75 percent of the granted lifetime. The runtime recomputes it after every success and after every allow-expiry through normal_refresh_at, so the refresh point drifts later on each pass and creeps toward the expiry. The doc comment above the function contradicts itself on exactly this point. The claim that the refresh time always lies before the expiry also fails for an already expired credential, which yields a past time. The test at src/credential_set.rs:1218 records that behaviour as accepted, and RuntimeCredential::new at src/refresh.rs:226 applies no clamp.

[narrow-the-statement] The claim that the system writes a warning is false. ExpiryPolicy::on_credential_expired at src/credential_set.rs:244 only builds a message inside an enum value and returns it. The function has no caller anywhere outside its own module tests, and nothing in the run loop watches for expiry, so no operator ever sees the text. Stating that noscope only writes a warning describes behaviour that does not happen.

unsupported_recommendations.recommendation: Noscope may compare the credential value before and after a refresh to tell a renewal apart from a rotation. No consumer of that distinction exists today.
next_wake_delay returns the smallest remaining time across all scheduled credentials. A past-due credential maps to a zero delay. The function returns nothing when no credential exists.

uncertainty.rationale: Every verdict was formed by reading the cited sites at the pinned commit; several were confirmed by running the pinned binary.

contributions.strongest_finding: The wall-clock timeout is dead twice over: no flag sets it and the run loop wait path never reads the timeout field.

challenges.objection: [narrow-the-statement] The first sentence claims an unconditional guarantee. configure_child_for_run_mode is an empty no-op on every target other than Linux (src/process_group.rs:56-59), so both protections are Linux-only and the statement must say so for the group creation as well as for PDEATHSIG. The mint clause is also weaker than it reads: agent_process installs the pre_exec hook only for AgentMode::Run (src/agent_process.rs:116-127), so the ProcessGroupMode::Mint no-op branch has no production caller at all and is exercised only by the helper mint_mode_process_group_behavior. The rule shape survives: configure_child_for_mode is one function with one production call site and it realizes the whole obligation.

[narrow-the-statement] The code never reads the child's real process group identifier. forward_signal negates child.id() and kills that number (src/agent_process.rs:159-162). The negated child pid equals the process group only where the setpgid in pre_exec ran, which is Linux run mode. On other Unix targets the child stays in noscope's own group, so the first kill either fails with ESRCH or, worse, reaches an unrelated process group whose identifier happens to equal the child pid. The statement therefore overstates 'the whole child process group' and must name the assumption.

[narrow-the-statement] The SIGPIPE half of the statement has no enforcement path and is not reachable. cmd_run registers handlers for SIGTERM, SIGINT and SIGHUP only (src/main.rs:374-377), and parent_signal_from_raw maps nothing else (src/run_signal_wiring.rs:69-76). No production code ever constructs ParentSignal::Sigpipe, so both SIGPIPE branches, at signal_policy.rs:224 and signal_policy.rs:238, are dead outside unit tests. The Rust runtime already ignores SIGPIPE at startup, so the policy predicate restates a default it does not cause. A predicate proves a value exists, not that the system ignores a signal.

[demote-rule-to-requirement] The named symbol does not realize the obligation. dispatch_pending_parent_signals only iterates over raw values; the filter that drops unknown signals lives in parent_signal_from_raw, and the fact that only real deliveries enter the loop comes from the signal_hook registration of exactly three signals at src/main.rs:374-377. Three cooperating sites carry the guarantee, so this is a requirement with several sites, not a rule at one function. The evidence is also weaker than claimed: tests/noscope_f75_os_signal_wiring.rs drives integration_runtime::forward_sigterm_then_escalate, which is a second copy of the run loop, not cmd_run.

[demote-rule-to-requirement] One clause is false and the rule spans two functions. abandon_revocation is set at src/signal_policy.rs:251 and read nowhere outside tests, so the system does not give up further cleanup. Cleanup cannot be abandoned anyway, because revocation runs synchronously inside the handling of the first signal and finishes before the loop reads a second signal. The obligation also needs two sites: signal_policy holds the shutdown_started state and returns the decision, while run_signal_wiring sends the actual SIGKILL at line 52. on_shutdown_signal alone kills nothing.

[demote-rule-to-requirement] The named type does not realize the obligation on its own. RunSignalWiring holds the latch, but the run loop must consult revoke_attempted() at src/main.rs:401 before the exit path revokes. If cmd_run ignored that query, the same run would revoke twice, so the guarantee lives in two cooperating sites. The latch is also weaker than stated: revoke_attempted is set only after revoke_all returns Ok (src/run_signal_wiring.rs:47-50). A failing revoke propagates out of dispatch_pending_parent_signals, so cmd_run aborts with exit 70, never retries, and leaves the child process running and unreaped.

[narrow-the-statement] The second sentence is false as written. cmd_run starts revocation with no signal and no child exit on two paths: after a partial mint failure at src/main.rs:190 and after a child spawn failure at src/main.rs:369. The cited negative evidence is also empty. run_mode_poll_without_signal_for_test at src/main.rs:416-429 is a cfg(test) stub that ignores its arguments and returns signal_processed false as a constant, so the tests at src/main.rs:1754 and src/main.rs:1775 assert nothing about the real loop. The f75 test drives the shadow runtime in integration_runtime, not cmd_run.

[demote-rule-to-requirement] terminate_group_for_mode has no production caller. The only caller is the module's own test helper terminate_run_mode_group_and_report at src/process_group.rs:216, and the grandchildren test proves the helper, not the product. cmd_run never terminates a group on any exit path, so an orphaned grandchild keeps the injected credentials until the TTL expires. The named function therefore cannot realize the obligation, which needs a caller in the run exit path that knows the process group. The pgid rejection clause is an implementation detail of a private helper and does not belong in a requirement.

[reclassify-as-speculation] The evidence proves a constant exists, not that anything enforces it. shutdown_grace_period() has exactly one caller in the whole repository, the trailing assertion at src/signal_policy.rs:393 inside the NS-026 forwarding test. No code anywhere waits a period and then sends SIGKILL to the agent child. The claim that an operator can change the period is plainly false, because grace_period is private, has no setter, no CLI flag and no config key. The only real grace period in the system is the 5 second SIGTERM to SIGKILL wait for provider commands in provider_exec, which is a different subject. No README section, document, or draft states a child grace period obligation, so this reads as a test-driven artifact rather than a requirement.

[reclassify-as-speculation] The feature is dead in two independent ways, so no obligation is enforced. First, no CLI flag sets a limit and cmd_run always passes timeout None at src/main.rs:364. Second, and stronger, even a non-None timeout would be ignored, because the run loop waits with try_wait_exit_code at src/main.rs:398 and that method never reads the timeout field. wait_child_with_optional_timeout is reachable only from wait_for_exit_status and wait_capture_with_revoke, and neither has a production caller anywhere in the binary. Adding a flag alone would not switch the behaviour on. No README section, document, or draft states a wall clock limit obligation, so this is a test-driven artifact of NS-057.

[reclassify-as-speculation] AgentProcessError::exit_code() has no production caller. cmd_run formats the spawn error with Display and wraps it as Error::internal (src/main.rs:368-371), which the NS-054 taxonomy maps to 70. No test asserts the binary's exit status for a missing or non-executable command. The spawn failure test at src/main.rs:1706 only asserts is_err(). The documented contract points the other way: src/exit_code.rs:70-76 states that noscope uses sysexits values for its own failures and passes the child code through only when the child ran. A child that never started is a noscope failure under that contract, so 127 and 126 form an unadopted shell convention rather than a stated obligation.

[narrow-the-statement] The phrase 'the child' is too broad and the statement as written is contradicted elsewhere in the system. Provider mint and revoke commands are also child processes of noscope, and they deliberately receive NOSCOPE_PROVIDER, NOSCOPE_ROLE and NOSCOPE_TOKEN_ID (src/main.rs:140-141 and src/provider_exec.rs). The rule holds only for the command that AgentProcess::spawn starts. With that scope named, the rule survives the other two challenges.

unsupported_recommendations.recommendation: The system may allow the child a grace period after the first shutdown signal before it sends SIGKILL. No such wait exists in the code today.
The system may accept a wall clock limit for the child, kill the child at that limit, and report 128 plus 9. No limit reaches the run path today.
The system may exit 127 when the child command does not exist and 126 when the command is not executable. The run path exits 70 in both cases today.

uncertainty.rationale: Every verdict was formed by reading the cited sites at the pinned commit; several were confirmed by running the pinned binary.

contributions.strongest_finding: TokenProvider and CleanupOnDropFuture are abandoned-design artifacts, but the live abandon path is unguarded: a timed-out mint future is dropped with no kill_on_drop, so an orphaned provider can mint a credential noscope never sees.

challenges.objection: [narrow-the-statement] The statement claims every in-memory credential carries an expiry. The type only guarantees this for ScopedToken. The same credential also lives as a plain String in ProviderExecResult.stdout (src/provider_exec.rs:422) and in the child environment map built at src/main.rs:202-206. Neither copy carries an expiry. Narrow the claim to the type that actually enforces it.

[narrow-the-statement] The claim that the redacted form does not keep the raw credential value is too strong. For a non-JWT credential longer than 16 bytes, compute_redacted_form at src/redaction.rs:83 stores the first 8 characters of the credential in redacted_display. The struct therefore does keep part of the raw value, and that String has no Drop impl, so it survives in memory after the owning ScopedToken zeroizes.

[narrow-the-statement] Two words hide the behaviour. First, the code always shows the eight-character prefix for a long non-JWT credential, so the word may is wrong and it conceals an unconditional partial disclosure. Second, the word completely overstates the short and JWT branches, because hash_based_id derives the shown identifier from the credential value itself when no provider identifier exists.

[demote-to-detail] Apply the rewrite test. Replace hash_based_id with a per-process counter or a random identifier and no system behaviour changes. Nothing consumes the digest. Revocation uses the metadata token_id, which the live mint paths set to tok-<provider> at src/main.rs:161 and src/main.rs:704, never the hash. The only thing that asserts stability is the unit test at src/redaction.rs:267, which has no production consumer. Stability across runs is therefore a property of one display helper, not an obligation of the system. It is also a liability: a truncated SHA-256 of a short credential is an offline brute-force oracle for that credential.

[narrow-the-statement] The evidence supports four named types, not the universal claim. ProviderExecResult (src/provider_exec.rs:419) derives Debug and holds the raw provider JSON in a public stdout String, so its debug output prints the credential in full. Provider stderr also reaches an error message unredacted: at src/main.rs:864-877 execute_revoke embeds exec_result.stderr into the returned error and into the emitted event, and redact_stderr (src/provider_exec.rs:342) only removes values of environment keys starting with NOSCOPE_TOKEN, which the revoke path sets to the empty string and the mint path never sets at all. No automated check exists either: src/ci_checks.rs only asserts that workflow files exist.

[narrow-the-statement] The cluster records no contest, but the run command carries raw credentials on a second channel. CredentialSet::env_map (src/credential_set.rs:300-305) calls expose_secret for every credential, and src/main.rs:202-212 hands that map to the child process as its environment. The child environment is the whole purpose of run mode and NS-012 names it as the approved delivery route, so it is deliberate. The statement as written declares mint standard output the single raw channel, and that is false.

[narrow-the-statement] The evidence proves that one type refuses one trait. static_assertions on ScopedToken (src/token.rs:283) shows ScopedToken is not Serialize. It does not show that the program never writes a credential to disk. The credential is in fact serialized: SerializableMintEnvelope (src/mint.rs:60) derives Serialize over a raw &str token, and MintEnvelope::to_json renders it. Both README.md:72 and docs/QUICKSTART.md:57 then tell the operator to redirect that output into mint.json. Persistence is one shell redirection away and the project documents it.

[narrow-the-statement] The universal claim fails on a live type. ProviderExecResult (src/provider_exec.rs:419-433) holds the raw provider JSON in a public stdout field and derives Debug, so it is a secret-holding type whose debug output shows the value. It also has no Drop impl. The three checked types are ScopedToken, CredentialSet and MintEnvelope, and the assertions cover only Clone and Serialize on the first two. Nothing in the build stops the next author from adding a credential field to a type that derives Debug, because src/ci_checks.rs checks workflow files only.

[narrow-the-statement] The second sentence is false. Several copies of the credential have no owner that wipes them. ProviderExecResult.stdout keeps the raw provider JSON and has no Drop impl. The environment map built at src/main.rs:202-206 copies every secret into an owned HashMap<String, String> that is never zeroized and is then handed to the child. The redacted prefix inside RedactedToken keeps eight characters of a long credential and is never wiped. Three named types do zeroize, and the statement should claim only that.

[reclassify-as-speculation] No warning exists. The flag reaches a dead end. provider_output_to_scoped_token_with_metadata (src/token_convert.rs:74) is the only reader of the flag and it has no caller outside its own test module. Both live mint paths call the plain provider_output_to_scoped_token instead, at src/main.rs:158 and src/main.rs:701, which drops the flag on the floor. A grep across src for any stderr write about a computed or non-authoritative expiry finds nothing. The evidence is two comments stating intent plus a struct field that no production code reads, and that is intent, not behaviour.

[narrow-the-statement] The claim that every minted credential carries an identifier is not enforced anywhere. MintEnvelope::from_scoped_token falls back to an empty string at src/mint.rs:95, MintEnvelope::new accepts an empty identifier, and RevokeInput::from_mint_json (src/mint.rs:151) accepts an empty token_id as long as the field is present. The identifier is also not a credential identifier in practice. Both live paths synthesize tok-<provider> at src/main.rs:161 and src/main.rs:704, so it identifies the provider and not the credential, and two credentials from one provider collide. The part the code does support is the independence of revocation from the credential value.

[reclassify-as-speculation] This is an artifact of an abandoned design. CleanupOnDropFuture and with_mint_cleanup have no caller anywhere except src/lib.rs:67, which re-exports them, and their own tests at src/token_provider.rs:302 to 369. They exist to serve TokenProvider::mint, which returns a boxed future, and no production type implements TokenProvider. The live abandon case runs through a different mechanism entirely: mint_all wraps each provider future in tokio::time::timeout at src/orchestrator.rs:70, and on elapse it drops the future and returns a plain MintResult::Failure with no cleanup at all. Naming this dead future as the rule symbol asserts an enforcement that the running program does not have.

[reclassify-as-speculation] The statement describes a design the system abandoned. No production type implements TokenProvider, and the only implementors are DummyProvider and CleanupAwareProvider inside the test module of the same file. The real system reaches a provider as a subprocess through execute_provider_command, and it models a provider as ResolvedProvider (src/provider.rs:201) holding command strings. That model contradicts the statement in two ways. First, only mint_cmd is mandatory, while refresh_cmd and revoke_cmd are Option and default to absent, so a provider need not offer refresh or revoke at all. Second, the shipped binary never runs a refresh command: main.rs mentions refresh_cmd only to print it in diagnostic output at src/main.rs:1119.

[narrow-the-statement] The never claim fails on the revoke failure path. At src/main.rs:864-877 execute_revoke takes the provider stderr and puts it verbatim into both the returned error message and the emitted RevokeFail event. The redaction that runs over that stderr is weaker than it looks: redact_stderr (src/provider_exec.rs:342) removes only the values of environment keys starting with NOSCOPE_TOKEN, it skips empty values, and the revoke path sets NOSCOPE_TOKEN to the empty string (src/main.rs:836). No token value is ever removed from revoke stderr. The mint path never sets a NOSCOPE_TOKEN variable either, so the same passthrough applies there. The messages noscope writes itself are clean, but the messages noscope relays are not.

unsupported_recommendations.recommendation: A credential may carry no provider identifier. The redaction helper then builds a fallback identifier from the first eight bytes of the SHA-256 digest of the credential. The same credential always yields the same identifier.
A provider may report no expiry. The system should then tell the operator that it computed the expiry itself. The system should also state that this expiry is not authoritative.
The system may abandon a mint before the mint finishes. The system should then run a cleanup step, because the provider may have already created a credential.
A provider should support minting, refreshing and revoking a credential. A refresh should return a new credential and should leave the old credential unchanged.

uncertainty.rationale: Every verdict was formed by reading the cited sites at the pinned commit; several were confirmed by running the pinned binary.

contributions.strongest_finding: 131 merged candidates survived dedup across seven partitions; the adversarial pass upheld or narrowed 116 and reclassified 15 as speculation, with one genuine design fork (the revoke contract) left contested for human disposition.

material_claims.statement: A mint over several providers succeeds only when every provider returns a credential. On any provider failure the system produces no credential set and revokes every credential it already minted.
The mint command writes one JSON array on a single line with one envelope per minted credential. When any provider fails the command writes nothing to standard output.
The helper validate_env_key_uniqueness rejects a credential list that repeats an environment variable name and it names every conflicting provider. The mint and run commands never call this helper.
The orchestrator applies its own timeout to each provider mint attempt. The run and mint commands set that timeout to 30 seconds. A provider that exceeds the timeout becomes a failed provider.
A provider timeout error names the provider and the configured timeout in whole seconds. The message does not report the measured elapsed time.
The orchestrator holds a semaphore permit for each provider mint attempt, so concurrent attempts never exceed the configured limit. The run and mint commands set that limit to 8.
The orchestration waits for a result from every requested provider before it decides success or failure. It does not cancel other providers after the first failure, so the rollback list is complete.

In run mode every provider mint attempt emits a start event and then one success or failure event. The closing event carries the provider, the duration, and the token identifier or the error text. The mint command installs no event emitter, so it emits nothing.

The run rollback revokes each token under a separate 5 second wall clock budget and at most 3 retries. Delays start at 100 milliseconds and double. The rollback handles tokens one after another, so the total rollback time grows with the token count. A zero budget skips revocation, but no production caller passes zero.

Every rollback revocation attempt writes one log line to standard error. The line names the provider, the credential identifier, the expiry, the attempt number, and the reason when the attempt failed.

Signal revocation gives each credential a 10 second wall clock budget and at most 3 retries. Waits start at 500 milliseconds and double. The code checks the budget only between attempts, so one slow attempt can run past the budget.

The run command revokes every active credential in parallel when the child exits or a shutdown signal arrives. A failure for one credential does not stop the others. A panicking task yields no result, so the report can be shorter than the credential list.

A revoke command that exits with status 0 counts as success. The provider script decides whether an already revoked credential exits 0. No production code inspects revoke stderr for already revoked or expired text.
The mint command and the run command reject a missing TTL on the flag path. They reject a TTL below 60 seconds. They reject a TTL above 43200 seconds. They exit with code 64.
The mint command and the run command reject a role that holds any character outside ASCII letters, digits, hyphens, underscores, and dots. This check runs on the flag path before provider resolution.
A mint request must carry at least one provider, a non-empty role, and a valid TTL. Noscope must check the request before it resolves or runs any provider.
The mint command refuses to write credentials when stdout is a terminal. It exits with code 64. The --force-terminal flag overrides the refusal.
Every envelope in the mint stdout JSON array carries exactly five fields. The fields are token, expires_at, token_id, provider, and role. The expires_at field uses RFC 3339 form.
The revoke command takes the credential from --token-id together with --provider, or from a mint envelope on stdin. The two forms exclude each other.
The revoke command reads one JSON object from stdin. It keeps only the token_id field and the provider field. It discards the raw credential value. It rejects an object that lacks either kept field.

The noscope binary revokes a credential using the credential identifier and the provider name alone. The binary never passes the credential value to a revoke command. A provider that needs the credential value cannot revoke through the binary.

A revoke command receives NOSCOPE_TOKEN and NOSCOPE_TOKEN_ID from the environment. A revoke command never receives NOSCOPE_TTL. The caller decides what value NOSCOPE_TOKEN holds. The binary sets NOSCOPE_TOKEN to an empty string.
The revoke command must reject any command line that carries a raw credential flag. The command line must still accept the opaque identifier flag.

A credential reaches a child process or a provider command only through an environment variable. No code path places a credential in a command argument. The mint command may still write a credential to stdout.
Noscope must disable core dumps before it loads any credential. It must set the soft limit and the hard limit to zero. A command must abort with a security error when the platform refuses.
A ScopedToken always carries an expiry time. Both constructors take a non-optional DateTime, so the program cannot build a credential object without an expiry.

A RedactedToken stores only a display string that the constructor computes once. It never stores the whole credential. For a long credential the stored string still contains the first eight characters.

The system hides all characters of a JWT credential and of any credential of sixteen bytes or fewer. It shows an identifier instead. For every other credential the system always shows the first eight characters followed by three dots.
Every type that holds a credential and defines Display or Debug prints the redacted form instead of the value. No flag and no environment variable turns redaction off.

The system releases a raw credential on exactly two channels. Mint writes the credential to standard output. Run injects the credential into the environment of the child process. Every other channel shows the redacted form.

The noscope process never opens a file to write a credential value. The process keeps a credential in memory, prints it to standard output during mint, and passes it to a child process environment during run.
The core credential types refuse Clone and refuse Serialize, and they redact their debug output. These types are ScopedToken, CredentialSet, MintEnvelope and ProviderOutput.
The credential-holding types wipe their secret material when they drop. ScopedToken, MintEnvelope and ProviderOutput each implement Drop and zeroize the credential value.

Provider output becomes an in-memory credential through one conversion function. The function attaches the role, the provider name and a credential identifier that the caller supplies, and it keeps the expiry that the parser produced.
When a provider omits the expiry, the system sets the expiry to the current time plus the requested time to live. The system records that the provider did not supply the expiry.
The revoke path needs only a credential identifier and a provider name. The system passes an empty value for the credential itself when it runs a revoke command.
An error message that noscope composes itself names only a location, a provider name or an opaque identifier. It never contains the credential value.

A provider mint command must print a JSON object with a token field that holds a non-empty string. The system rejects output that has no such token field. When the output carries an expires_at field, that field must be a valid ISO 8601 timestamp. The system accepts an expires_at timestamp that lies in the past, to tolerate provider clock skew. When expires_at is absent or null, the system computes the expiry from the requested TTL.
The system accepts a minted credential only when the provider command exits with code 0. Output that looks valid but arrives with a non-zero exit produces a mint failure instead of a credential.

The system runs a provider command as a direct argv execution and never hands the command string to a shell. An operator may still name a shell as the provider command, and then substituted values reach that shell as program text. The system validates role characters only when the operator passes --role, not when the role comes from a profile.

The system replaces {role} and {ttl} in every argument of a provider mint command before it runs that command. The system performs no substitution on a revoke command. An unknown placeholder such as {unknown} stays in the argument unchanged.

The user documentation must show the placeholder form that the system really substitutes. The documentation currently shows {{role}} and {{ttl}} while the system substitutes {role} and {ttl}. A configuration copied from the documentation therefore passes the role and the TTL wrapped in braces to the provider. Either the documentation or the substitution set must change.
The system gives the TTL to a provider command as a plain integer count of seconds with no unit suffix.

The system stops a provider command that runs past its time limit. It sends SIGTERM to the command and then sends SIGKILL after a grace period. Every live call site sets the limit to 30 seconds and the grace period to 5 seconds. The system signals only the direct child process, so a process that the provider started can survive.

The system labels a timed-out provider command with provider exit code 4, which means unavailable. Only the revoke path reads that label. The mint path reports a timeout message instead and ignores the label. The label does not change the exit status that noscope itself returns.

The system rejects provider standard output that is larger than 1 mebibyte and mints no credential from it. Output of exactly 1 mebibyte is accepted. The system reads the whole output into memory before it applies this check, so the check does not bound memory use.
The system keeps at most 4096 bytes of provider standard error. The cut never splits a UTF-8 character.

The system replaces the value of every variable whose name starts with NOSCOPE_TOKEN with the text [redacted] in captured provider standard error. No live command passes a credential value in such a variable, so this replacement removes nothing today. The system never redacts the credential that the provider itself printed. The system truncates standard error before it redacts, so a value that straddles the cut can leave a prefix behind.

A provider command starts with an empty environment. The system then sets PATH, HOME and LANG from its own environment. The system also sets the variables it injects and the variables from the provider configuration env table. No other parent variable reaches the provider. When PATH, HOME or LANG are unset, the system uses /usr/bin:/bin, /root and C.UTF-8.

A provider process reports its result through its exit code. Code 0 means success and code 1 means a general error. Code 2 means an authentication failure and code 3 means a role that does not exist. Code 4 means an unavailable provider. The system reports codes 2, 3 and 4 inside the failure message and takes no different action on them. The revoke path treats only code 0 as success.

The system treats a provider exit code outside 0 to 4 as a general error. When the raw code is above 128 the system also records the signal number as the code minus 128. A raw code of exactly 128 records no signal number. A process that a signal really killed reports no code, so the system substitutes 1 and records no signal number.
A provider process that a signal killed counts as a failure. The system mints no credential from that process, even when the process already printed valid JSON.

The system reads provider standard output and standard error concurrently while it waits for the process to exit. A provider that writes more than the pipe buffer therefore still finishes. The system waits for both reads without a time limit after the process exits.
The system reports a failure when it cannot start a provider executable. It mints no credential in that case.
A provider that declares support for refresh or revoke must also configure the matching command. The system rejects an inconsistent provider configuration when it parses the configuration file.

The system accepts a provider or profile name only when every character is an ASCII letter, digit, hyphen, underscore, or dot. The system rejects the empty name. The system rejects the names dot and double dot.
The system reports any rejected provider or profile name as a security error. The system does not report a rejected name as a configuration error.

The system refuses to read a provider or profile configuration file that is group-writable or grants any permission to other users. The same check covers both file kinds. The check runs before the system reads the file content.

Provider commands come from exactly one configuration layer. Direct overrides beat environment variables. Environment variables beat the configuration file. The system never merges values from two layers. A winning override layer can leave the mint command empty without an error.
The system reads provider command overrides from NOSCOPE_MINT_CMD, NOSCOPE_REFRESH_CMD, and NOSCOPE_REVOKE_CMD. The system treats an empty variable as unset.

When no configuration layer supplies a provider, the system reports the provider as not found. The error lists three fixed candidate locations. Those locations are a command-line flag, an environment variable, and a configuration file path.

A provider configuration file must declare contract_version and a commands table with a non-empty mint command. The system rejects a provider file that lacks either of those fields. The system ignores keys it does not recognise.

The system accepts a provider contract version only when that version is in the supported set. The supported set holds the current version and the version before it. The error names the supported versions. The system checks the version only for a provider that comes from a configuration file.
A missing provider configuration file is not an error by itself. The system treats that layer as absent. The system then resolves the provider from the remaining sources.

The system stops with an error when a provider or profile file is malformed. The system never mints credentials from a file it could only partly understand. The reported error kind differs between the two file kinds.

The system reads a named provider from noscope/providers/<name>.toml under the config home. The system reads a named profile from noscope/profiles/<name>.toml under the config home. The run, mint, doctor, and init commands take the config home from XDG_CONFIG_HOME, or from the .config directory inside HOME when that variable is unset. The revoke, validate, and dry-run commands ignore XDG_CONFIG_HOME.

A profile must list at least one credential. Each credential must give a non-empty provider name. Each credential must give a non-empty role. Each credential must give a whole-number TTL greater than zero.

A profile credential accepts only the fields provider, role, ttl, and env_key. The system rejects any other field inside a credential. The system ignores unknown fields at the top level of a profile. No part of the system implements profile inheritance, override, or nesting.

The system reports every schema problem it finds inside the credential entries of a profile in one error message. The system does not stop at the first bad credential. The system still fails early on a syntax error or a missing credentials section.
A profile that the operator names must exist. The system reports an error that includes the path when the named profile file is missing.

The profile option is a complete alternative to the provider, role, and TTL options. The system rejects a command that mixes the two forms. The system rejects a run or a mint that supplies neither form.

Each credential in a profile reaches the child process under an environment variable name. The profile may set that name with env_key. When the profile does not set it, the system builds a name from the upper-case provider name and the position in the list. The system does not reject two credentials that declare the same env_key.

The validate command checks the mint, refresh, and revoke commands of one resolved provider. It treats each whole command string as a filesystem path. It reports every command that is not an existing executable file. It collects all problems together and names the command type and the string. It runs none of those commands.
The dry-run command prints the provider name, the configuration source, the mint, refresh and revoke commands, the role, the TTL, and the provider environment map. It runs no provider command.

The doctor command first checks that the noscope config directory exists. When that directory exists, doctor checks each TOML file directly inside the providers subdirectory. Doctor also checks each mint, refresh, and revoke command that such a file configures. Doctor stops after the first check when the config directory is missing.

Doctor reports a missing or non-executable provider command as a warning, because the configuration is correct while the machine setup is not. Doctor reports an unreadable provider file, a malformed provider file, or insecure permissions on that file as a failure.
The doctor exit code shows the worst check status. All passing gives 0, warnings only give 1, and any failure gives 78.
The doctor command only reads the filesystem. It creates, changes, and deletes no file and no directory under the config home.

The init command creates the noscope directory and its providers and profiles subdirectories under the config home. It sets mode 0700 on each of those three directories after it creates that directory. It does not set the mode on any parent directory it creates. It does not tighten a directory that already exists.
A second run of the init command does not fail. It skips every path that is already a directory, so it does not change the permissions of an existing directory.
The run command mints every credential before it spawns the child process. When any mint fails, the run command returns an error and never spawns the child.
The run command passes minted credentials to the child only as environment variables. An injected variable silently replaces an inherited variable of the same name.

When the operator names providers with --provider, the run and mint commands place each credential in the environment variable <PROVIDER>_TOKEN. The provider name is upper-cased and is otherwise unchanged. A profile may set a different key for a credential.
The provider mint command receives the provider name in NOSCOPE_PROVIDER and the role in NOSCOPE_ROLE.

The system never runs a provider command that parses to no arguments. The single execution entry point rejects an empty argument list. The mint and revoke call sites reject it earlier and name the provider and the command type. The refresh call site produces a generic error instead.
The system splits a configured command string into arguments with POSIX shell quoting rules and keeps a quoted segment as one argument. On unbalanced quoting it falls back to whitespace splitting.
The system maps a child exit status to a single integer. A normal exit gives the exact child exit code. A signal death gives 128 plus the signal number. Any other status gives 1.

The run supervisor keeps the parent process alive until the child exits. It polls for pending shutdown signals every 20 milliseconds and hands each one to the signal wiring. It returns the child exit code when the child exits.

On Linux the system places every run mode child in a new process group that the child leads. On Linux the kernel also sends SIGTERM to that child when noscope dies first. Other platforms apply neither protection. Mint mode applies neither protection.

The system forwards a run mode signal to the process group whose identifier equals the child process identifier. The system signals the child alone when that group does not exist. The system treats a missing target as a completed forward.
The system forwards SIGTERM, SIGINT, and SIGHUP to the child process group. The system ignores every other signal the operating system delivers.

The system starts a shutdown only after the operating system delivers SIGTERM, SIGINT, or SIGHUP. The system never creates a shutdown signal by itself. The system ignores every other delivered signal.
The first shutdown signal starts a graceful shutdown. A second SIGTERM or SIGINT makes the system send SIGKILL to the child at once. A second SIGHUP does not escalate.
The system attempts revocation at most once during a run. The first shutdown signal makes that attempt. The exit path attempts revocation only when no signal already attempted it.
The system emits a signal_received event for every shutdown signal it handles. The system emits a signal_forwarded event only after a forward succeeds.
The first shutdown signal starts revocation of every credential in the run credential set. While the child runs, the system starts revocation only on a shutdown signal or on child exit.

In run mode the system tries to revoke every minted credential before the noscope process exits. This holds when the child exits normally, when the child cannot start, and when a shutdown signal arrives.
When a run ends the system terminates the whole child process group with SIGTERM so no descendant outlives the run. Mint mode never terminates process groups.
The system removes every environment variable whose name starts with NOSCOPE_ from the agent child environment. The system refuses to start the agent child when an injected key uses that prefix.

The system writes every JSON event as one compact line. EventEmitter::format_event produces every line that the system emits. A text event may break across lines when the error message contains a line break.

Every event carries a timestamp in RFC 3339 form, a snake case type name, and a scope name. An event may also carry a token identifier, a duration in milliseconds, an exit code, a signal number, and an error message. Absent optional fields appear as null in the JSON form.

The run command emits an event for the start, the success, and the failure of each mint and refresh action. It also emits events for child spawn, child exit, signal receipt, and signal forwarding. The other commands build the same events but discard them because they install no emitter.
The system writes all events to standard error and never to standard output. In run mode standard output belongs to the child alone.

No call site writes a credential value into an event. The token field carries a plain token identifier. No type or function prevents a caller from writing a secret into the token field or the error field.
The log format parser accepts only the lowercase words json and text. It rejects every other value, including any other capitalization.
Every failure that the Error type carries names one category from a closed set of six. The categories are usage, config, provider, security, profile, and internal.
Each error category maps to one fixed process exit code. Usage and security give 64. Provider gives 65. Profile gives 66. Internal gives 70. Config gives 78. Success gives 0.

When a command returns an error and the operator selected JSON output, main writes one JSON object to standard error. The object carries the status, the command name, the error kind, and the message. In text mode main writes one line that starts with noscope and a colon.
The validate, dry-run, mint, revoke, and init commands write their success message to standard output. These five commands write nothing to standard error when they succeed.
In JSON output mode the dry-run, validate, and revoke commands each write one JSON object to standard output. Each object carries an ok status, the command name, and the provider.

When a revoke command fails, the failure message that reaches the operator includes the text that the provider wrote to standard error. The mint path discards provider standard error and reports the exit code alone.
The completions command writes a shell completion script to standard output. It accepts every shell that the completion library defines, which includes bash, zsh, and fish.

The binary hands help output, version output, and argument parse errors to the argument parser, which prints them and exits. The parser writes help and version text to standard output and exits 0. It writes a usage error and exits 2.
Help text speaks to operators. It carries concrete run, mint, and revoke examples. It explains that the profile flag excludes the credential flags. It never shows internal rule identifiers.
The failure codes in the NoscopeExitCode set start at 64 and never collide with the provider protocol codes 1 to 4. The doctor command and the argument parser return values outside that set.
The product must not present a safety behaviour as working when it does not yet hold. The operator documentation separates the behaviour that works today from the behaviour that remains planned.
The system rests on three safety layers. These are process group termination, revocation at exit, and expiry by TTL.
A failed credential refresh never stops the child process. Noscope retries the refresh with growing delays. After the retries run out noscope lets the credential expire on its own.

Refresh retries start at 1 second and double on each attempt. Noscope stops after 4 retries. Each retry delay varies by up to 25 percent. Noscope skips a retry whose delay exceeds half of the credential lifetime that remains.
Noscope tracks refresh failures separately for each credential. A failure on one credential never changes the retry state of another credential.
A run of failed refreshes never disables refresh for good. The credential returns to its normal refresh time after the failure window. The next attempt always waits at least 1 second.
Noscope runs a refresh command only for credentials whose refresh time has arrived. Noscope runs no refresh command after the child process exits.

A provider refresh command receives the current credential value and the credential identifier. The command also receives the credential lifetime in whole seconds. The provider uses these values to renew that exact lease.

Noscope warns at startup whenever rotate mode is active. The warning states that noscope injects environment variables once at spawn time. The warning states that the running child never sees a refreshed credential.

Noscope computes a refresh time for each credential from that credential's own expiry. The refresh time falls at 75 percent of the granted lifetime. Noscope never merges credentials into one shared schedule.
The expiry of one credential must not stop the child process. The expiry must not trigger a new mint. Noscope must warn the operator and name the provider and the token identifier.
Every failed refresh produces a warning for the operator. Noscope emits that warning even when it still plans a retry.
The binary revoke path and the drafted provider contract disagree about whether a revoke command receives the credential value.

risks: Statements about unwired subsystems (refresh, group termination) describe designed rather than shipped behaviour and are marked as such in their summaries.

uncertainty.rationale: Every claim carries file and line evidence at the pinned commit and survived a dedicated adversarial refutation pass; several were confirmed by executing the pinned binary.

synthesis_packets.summary: Swarm backtrace of noscope at commit 9846669: seven extractors produced 274 candidates, merged to 131 clusters, adversarially refuted in nine batches. 117 proposals land (91 rule candidates and requirement candidates asserted, 2 contested on the revoke-contract fork, 1 asserted question). 15 clusters reclassified as speculation. Recurring pattern: obligations stated and tested at module level whose enforcement never reached a live command path.

consensus.statement: A multi-provider mint is all-or-nothing with rollback in run mode, but cmd_mint propagates the failure without revoking succeeded tokens, so mint mode leaks credentials on partial failure.

TTL bounds and role character validation are enforced on the flag path only. The profile path bypasses both, confirmed by executing the pinned binary with ttl 1 and a role holding shell metacharacters.
The documentation teaches double-brace placeholders while the binary substitutes single-brace forms, so a config copied from the docs passes brace-wrapped values to the provider.

A stratum of stated security obligations is dead code: the argv token scan, revoke-argument validation, profile validation, revoke idempotency classification, stderr verbose policy, the refresh subsystem, and process-group termination on exit all lack any live caller.

The stderr redaction pass removes nothing in production because its candidate list is built only from NOSCOPE_TOKEN environment values that no live command populates with a secret, and the credential the provider itself printed is never a candidate.
Only the run command installs an event emitter, so the standalone mint and revoke commands construct lifecycle events and silently discard them.

The NS rule identifier scheme collided: NS-080 and NS-081 each carry two unrelated meanings and NS-079 is asserted in tests but defined nowhere, so the previous verification ledger cannot be trusted as a registry.

contested_claims.statement: The noscope binary revokes a credential using the credential identifier and the provider name alone. The binary never passes the credential value to a revoke command. A provider that needs the credential value cannot revoke through the binary.

A revoke command receives NOSCOPE_TOKEN and NOSCOPE_TOKEN_ID from the environment. A revoke command never receives NOSCOPE_TTL. The caller decides what value NOSCOPE_TOKEN holds. The binary sets NOSCOPE_TOKEN to an empty string.

evidence_gaps.question: Is the missing rollback in mint mode intended, or must cmd_mint revoke succeeded tokens as cmd_run does?
Should profile-supplied roles and TTLs receive the same validation as flag-supplied ones, or are profile files trusted input?
Ship or delete: the refresh subsystem (560 unwired production lines) and process-group termination on exit (README safety layer one, no production caller).
No test exercises the production run supervisor loop end to end; the once-only revoke test drives the wiring through a cfg(test) helper.

unsupported_speculation.statement: The mint command ignores the global --output flag. The mint command always writes the same JSON envelope array. No artifact records whether anyone chose this behaviour.

A credential may carry no provider identifier. The redaction helper then builds a fallback identifier from the first eight bytes of the SHA-256 digest of the credential. The same credential always yields the same identifier.
A provider may report no expiry. The system should then tell the operator that it computed the expiry itself. The system should also state that this expiry is not authoritative.
The system may abandon a mint before the mint finishes. The system should then run a cleanup step, because the provider may have already created a credential.
A provider should support minting, refreshing and revoking a credential. A refresh should return a new credential and should leave the old credential unchanged.

The intended behavior is that the system discards provider standard error after a success unless the operator passes --verbose. The system always keeps standard error after a failure. The code does not implement the success half of this behavior. StderrPolicy has no production caller and the verbose flag never reaches a stderr decision.

The intended refresh contract gives the provider the credential, the credential identifier and the TTL in seconds through environment variables. Refresh output is meant to follow the same JSON contract as mint output. No refresh subcommand exists, so no operator can reach this contract. Only the shadow integration runtime calls the environment builder.
Extra environment variables declared in a provider file reach the provider command only when the file is the winning configuration layer.
The resolved-provider map holds one entry for each provider name. When two credentials name the same provider, the system keeps the first resolved configuration and discards the second.
The system may allow the child a grace period after the first shutdown signal before it sends SIGKILL. No such wait exists in the code today.
The system may accept a wall clock limit for the child, kill the child at that limit, and report 128 plus 9. No limit reaches the run path today.
The system may exit 127 when the child command does not exist and 126 when the command is not executable. The run path exits 70 in both cases today.
The run path names every failed provider in one joined message. The library can represent several failures as separate typed errors. No production code path uses that representation today.
Noscope may compare the credential value before and after a refresh to tell a renewal apart from a rotation. No consumer of that distinction exists today.
next_wake_delay returns the smallest remaining time across all scheduled credentials. A past-due credential maps to a zero delay. The function returns nothing when no credential exists.

dry-run prints provider [commands.env] values unredacted in both output modes.
