The terminal-refusal error names --force but the flag is --force-terminal.
The documented pipeline 'noscope mint | noscope revoke --from-stdin' fails because mint emits an array and revoke parses a single object.
Provider grandchildren survive both the provider timeout escalation and signal forwarding on non-Linux targets.
Exit codes 69, 77 and 79 are defined but unreachable; doctor exits 1 and clap exits 2, both outside the sysexits scheme.

suggested_artifacts.summary: A mint over several providers succeeds only when every provider returns a credential. On any provider failure the system produces no credential set and revokes every credential it already minted.
The mint command writes one JSON array on a single line with one envelope per minted credential. When any provider fails the command writes nothing to standard output.
The helper validate_env_key_uniqueness rejects a credential list that repeats an environment variable name and it names every conflicting provider. The mint and run commands never call this helper.
The orchestrator applies its own timeout to each provider mint attempt. The run and mint commands set that timeout to 30 seconds. A provider that exceeds the timeout becomes a failed provider.
A provider timeout error names the provider and the configured timeout in whole seconds. The message does not report the measured elapsed time.
The orchestrator holds a semaphore permit for each provider mint attempt, so concurrent attempts never exceed the configured limit. The run and mint commands set that limit to 8.
The orchestration waits for a result from every requested provider before it decides success or failure. It does not cancel other providers after the first failure, so the rollback list is complete.

In run mode every provider mint attempt emits a start event and then one success or failure event. The closing event carries the provider, the duration, and the token identifier or the error text. The mint command installs no event emitter, so it emits nothing.

The run rollback revokes each token under a separate 5 second wall clock budget and at most 3 retries. Delays start at 100 milliseconds and double. The rollback handles tokens one after another, so the total rollback time grows with the token count. A zero budget skips revocation, but no production

Every rollback revocation attempt writes one log line to standard error. The line names the provider, the credential identifier, the expiry, the attempt number, and the reason when the attempt failed.

Signal revocation gives each credential a 10 second wall clock budget and at most 3 retries. Waits start at 500 milliseconds and double. The code checks the budget only between attempts, so one slow attempt can run past the budget.

The run command revokes every active credential in parallel when the child exits or a shutdown signal arrives. A failure for one credential does not stop the others. A panicking task yields no result, so the report can be shorter than the credential list.

A revoke command that exits with status 0 counts as success. The provider script decides whether an already revoked credential exits 0. No production code inspects revoke stderr for already revoked or expired text.
The mint command and the run command reject a missing TTL on the flag path. They reject a TTL below 60 seconds. They reject a TTL above 43200 seconds. They exit with code 64.
The mint command and the run command reject a role that holds any character outside ASCII letters, digits, hyphens, underscores, and dots. This check runs on the flag path before provider resolution.
A mint request must carry at least one provider, a non-empty role, and a valid TTL. Noscope must check the request before it resolves or runs any provider.
The mint command refuses to write credentials when stdout is a terminal. It exits with code 64. The --force-terminal flag overrides the refusal.
Every envelope in the mint stdout JSON array carries exactly five fields. The fields are token, expires_at, token_id, provider, and role. The expires_at field uses RFC 3339 form.
The revoke command takes the credential from --token-id together with --provider, or from a mint envelope on stdin. The two forms exclude each other.
The revoke command reads one JSON object from stdin. It keeps only the token_id field and the provider field. It discards the raw credential value. It rejects an object that lacks either kept field.

The noscope binary revokes a credential using the credential identifier and the provider name alone. The binary never passes the credential value to a revoke command. A provider that needs the credential value cannot revoke through the binary.

A revoke command receives NOSCOPE_TOKEN and NOSCOPE_TOKEN_ID from the environment. A revoke command never receives NOSCOPE_TTL. The caller decides what value NOSCOPE_TOKEN holds. The binary sets NOSCOPE_TOKEN to an empty string.
The revoke command must reject any command line that carries a raw credential flag. The command line must still accept the opaque identifier flag.

A credential reaches a child process or a provider command only through an environment variable. No code path places a credential in a command argument. The mint command may still write a credential to stdout.
Noscope must disable core dumps before it loads any credential. It must set the soft limit and the hard limit to zero. A command must abort with a security error when the platform refuses.
A ScopedToken always carries an expiry time. Both constructors take a non-optional DateTime, so the program cannot build a credential object without an expiry.

A RedactedToken stores only a display string that the constructor computes once. It never stores the whole credential. For a long credential the stored string still contains the first eight characters.

The system hides all characters of a JWT credential and of any credential of sixteen bytes or fewer. It shows an identifier instead. For every other credential the system always shows the first eight characters followed by three dots.
Every type that holds a credential and defines Display or Debug prints the redacted form instead of the value. No flag and no environment variable turns redaction off.

The system releases a raw credential on exactly two channels. Mint writes the credential to standard output. Run injects the credential into the environment of the child process. Every other channel shows the redacted form.

The noscope process never opens a file to write a credential value. The process keeps a credential in memory, prints it to standard output during mint, and passes it to a child process environment during run.
The core credential types refuse Clone and refuse Serialize, and they redact their debug output. These types are ScopedToken, CredentialSet, MintEnvelope and ProviderOutput.
The credential-holding types wipe their secret material when they drop. ScopedToken, MintEnvelope and ProviderOutput each implement Drop and zeroize the credential value.

Provider output becomes an in-memory credential through one conversion function. The function attaches the role, the provider name and a credential identifier that the caller supplies, and it keeps the expiry that the parser produced.
When a provider omits the expiry, the system sets the expiry to the current time plus the requested time to live. The system records that the provider did not supply the expiry.
The revoke path needs only a credential identifier and a provider name. The system passes an empty value for the credential itself when it runs a revoke command.
An error message that noscope composes itself names only a location, a provider name or an opaque identifier. It never contains the credential value.

A provider mint command must print a JSON object with a token field that holds a non-empty string. The system rejects output that has no such token field. When the output carries an expires_at field, that field must be a valid ISO 8601 timestamp. The system accepts an expires_at timestamp that lies
The system accepts a minted credential only when the provider command exits with code 0. Output that looks valid but arrives with a non-zero exit produces a mint failure instead of a credential.

The system runs a provider command as a direct argv execution and never hands the command string to a shell. An operator may still name a shell as the provider command, and then substituted values reach that shell as program text. The system validates role characters only when the operator passes --

The system replaces {role} and {ttl} in every argument of a provider mint command before it runs that command. The system performs no substitution on a revoke command. An unknown placeholder such as {unknown} stays in the argument unchanged.

The user documentation must show the placeholder form that the system really substitutes. The documentation currently shows {{role}} and {{ttl}} while the system substitutes {role} and {ttl}. A configuration copied from the documentation therefore passes the role and the TTL wrapped in braces to the
The system gives the TTL to a provider command as a plain integer count of seconds with no unit suffix.

The system stops a provider command that runs past its time limit. It sends SIGTERM to the command and then sends SIGKILL after a grace period. Every live call site sets the limit to 30 seconds and the grace period to 5 seconds. The system signals only the direct child process, so a process that the

The system labels a timed-out provider command with provider exit code 4, which means unavailable. Only the revoke path reads that label. The mint path reports a timeout message instead and ignores the label. The label does not change the exit status that noscope itself returns.

The system rejects provider standard output that is larger than 1 mebibyte and mints no credential from it. Output of exactly 1 mebibyte is accepted. The system reads the whole output into memory before it applies this check, so the check does not bound memory use.
The system keeps at most 4096 bytes of provider standard error. The cut never splits a UTF-8 character.

The system replaces the value of every variable whose name starts with NOSCOPE_TOKEN with the text [redacted] in captured provider standard error. No live command passes a credential value in such a variable, so this replacement removes nothing today. The system never redacts the credential that the

A provider command starts with an empty environment. The system then sets PATH, HOME and LANG from its own environment. The system also sets the variables it injects and the variables from the provider configuration env table. No other parent variable reaches the provider. When PATH, HOME or LANG ar

A provider process reports its result through its exit code. Code 0 means success and code 1 means a general error. Code 2 means an authentication failure and code 3 means a role that does not exist. Code 4 means an unavailable provider. The system reports codes 2, 3 and 4 inside the failure message

The system treats a provider exit code outside 0 to 4 as a general error. When the raw code is above 128 the system also records the signal number as the code minus 128. A raw code of exactly 128 records no signal number. A process that a signal really killed reports no code, so the system substitut
A provider process that a signal killed counts as a failure. The system mints no credential from that process, even when the process already printed valid JSON.

The system reads provider standard output and standard error concurrently while it waits for the process to exit. A provider that writes more than the pipe buffer therefore still finishes. The system waits for both reads without a time limit after the process exits.
The system reports a failure when it cannot start a provider executable. It mints no credential in that case.
A provider that declares support for refresh or revoke must also configure the matching command. The system rejects an inconsistent provider configuration when it parses the configuration file.

The system accepts a provider or profile name only when every character is an ASCII letter, digit, hyphen, underscore, or dot. The system rejects the empty name. The system rejects the names dot and double dot.
The system reports any rejected provider or profile name as a security error. The system does not report a rejected name as a configuration error.

The system refuses to read a provider or profile configuration file that is group-writable or grants any permission to other users. The same check covers both file kinds. The check runs before the system reads the file content.

Provider commands come from exactly one configuration layer. Direct overrides beat environment variables. Environment variables beat the configuration file. The system never merges values from two layers. A winning override layer can leave the mint command empty without an error.
The system reads provider command overrides from NOSCOPE_MINT_CMD, NOSCOPE_REFRESH_CMD, and NOSCOPE_REVOKE_CMD. The system treats an empty variable as unset.

When no configuration layer supplies a provider, the system reports the provider as not found. The error lists three fixed candidate locations. Those locations are a command-line flag, an environment variable, and a configuration file path.

A provider configuration file must declare contract_version and a commands table with a non-empty mint command. The system rejects a provider file that lacks either of those fields. The system ignores keys it does not recognise.

The system accepts a provider contract version only when that version is in the supported set. The supported set holds the current version and the version before it. The error names the supported versions. The system checks the version only for a provider that comes from a configuration file.
A missing provider configuration file is not an error by itself. The system treats that layer as absent. The system then resolves the provider from the remaining sources.

The system stops with an error when a provider or profile file is malformed. The system never mints credentials from a file it could only partly understand. The reported error kind differs between the two file kinds.

The system reads a named provider from noscope/providers/<name>.toml under the config home. The system reads a named profile from noscope/profiles/<name>.toml under the config home. The run, mint, doctor, and init commands take the config home from XDG_CONFIG_HOME, or from the .config directory insi

A profile must list at least one credential. Each credential must give a non-empty provider name. Each credential must give a non-empty role. Each credential must give a whole-number TTL greater than zero.

A profile credential accepts only the fields provider, role, ttl, and env_key. The system rejects any other field inside a credential. The system ignores unknown fields at the top level of a profile. No part of the system implements profile inheritance, override, or nesting.

The system reports every schema problem it finds inside the credential entries of a profile in one error message. The system does not stop at the first bad credential. The system still fails early on a syntax error or a missing credentials section.
A profile that the operator names must exist. The system reports an error that includes the path when the named profile file is missing.

The profile option is a complete alternative to the provider, role, and TTL options. The system rejects a command that mixes the two forms. The system rejects a run or a mint that supplies neither form.

Each credential in a profile reaches the child process under an environment variable name. The profile may set that name with env_key. When the profile does not set it, the system builds a name from the upper-case provider name and the position in the list. The system does not reject two credentials

The validate command checks the mint, refresh, and revoke commands of one resolved provider. It treats each whole command string as a filesystem path. It reports every command that is not an existing executable file. It collects all problems together and names the command type and the string. It run
The dry-run command prints the provider name, the configuration source, the mint, refresh and revoke commands, the role, the TTL, and the provider environment map. It runs no provider command.

The doctor command first checks that the noscope config directory exists. When that directory exists, doctor checks each TOML file directly inside the providers subdirectory. Doctor also checks each mint, refresh, and revoke command that such a file configures. Doctor stops after the first check whe

Doctor reports a missing or non-executable provider command as a warning, because the configuration is correct while the machine setup is not. Doctor reports an unreadable provider file, a malformed provider file, or insecure permissions on that file as a failure.
The doctor exit code shows the worst check status. All passing gives 0, warnings only give 1, and any failure gives 78.
The doctor command only reads the filesystem. It creates, changes, and deletes no file and no directory under the config home.

The init command creates the noscope directory and its providers and profiles subdirectories under the config home. It sets mode 0700 on each of those three directories after it creates that directory. It does not set the mode on any parent directory it creates. It does not tighten a directory that
A second run of the init command does not fail. It skips every path that is already a directory, so it does not change the permissions of an existing directory.
The run command mints every credential before it spawns the child process. When any mint fails, the run command returns an error and never spawns the child.
The run command passes minted credentials to the child only as environment variables. An injected variable silently replaces an inherited variable of the same name.

When the operator names providers with --provider, the run and mint commands place each credential in the environment variable <PROVIDER>_TOKEN. The provider name is upper-cased and is otherwise unchanged. A profile may set a different key for a credential.
The provider mint command receives the provider name in NOSCOPE_PROVIDER and the role in NOSCOPE_ROLE.

The system never runs a provider command that parses to no arguments. The single execution entry point rejects an empty argument list. The mint and revoke call sites reject it earlier and name the provider and the command type. The refresh call site produces a generic error instead.
The system splits a configured command string into arguments with POSIX shell quoting rules and keeps a quoted segment as one argument. On unbalanced quoting it falls back to whitespace splitting.
The system maps a child exit status to a single integer. A normal exit gives the exact child exit code. A signal death gives 128 plus the signal number. Any other status gives 1.

The run supervisor keeps the parent process alive until the child exits. It polls for pending shutdown signals every 20 milliseconds and hands each one to the signal wiring. It returns the child exit code when the child exits.

On Linux the system places every run mode child in a new process group that the child leads. On Linux the kernel also sends SIGTERM to that child when noscope dies first. Other platforms apply neither protection. Mint mode applies neither protection.

The system forwards a run mode signal to the process group whose identifier equals the child process identifier. The system signals the child alone when that group does not exist. The system treats a missing target as a completed forward.
The system forwards SIGTERM, SIGINT, and SIGHUP to the child process group. The system ignores every other signal the operating system delivers.

The system starts a shutdown only after the operating system delivers SIGTERM, SIGINT, or SIGHUP. The system never creates a shutdown signal by itself. The system ignores every other delivered signal.
The first shutdown signal starts a graceful shutdown. A second SIGTERM or SIGINT makes the system send SIGKILL to the child at once. A second SIGHUP does not escalate.
The system attempts revocation at most once during a run. The first shutdown signal makes that attempt. The exit path attempts revocation only when no signal already attempted it.
The system emits a signal_received event for every shutdown signal it handles. The system emits a signal_forwarded event only after a forward succeeds.
The first shutdown signal starts revocation of every credential in the run credential set. While the child runs, the system starts revocation only on a shutdown signal or on child exit.

In run mode the system tries to revoke every minted credential before the noscope process exits. This holds when the child exits normally, when the child cannot start, and when a shutdown signal arrives.
When a run ends the system terminates the whole child process group with SIGTERM so no descendant outlives the run. Mint mode never terminates process groups.
The system removes every environment variable whose name starts with NOSCOPE_ from the agent child environment. The system refuses to start the agent child when an injected key uses that prefix.

The system writes every JSON event as one compact line. EventEmitter::format_event produces every line that the system emits. A text event may break across lines when the error message contains a line break.

Every event carries a timestamp in RFC 3339 form, a snake case type name, and a scope name. An event may also carry a token identifier, a duration in milliseconds, an exit code, a signal number, and an error message. Absent optional fields appear as null in the JSON form.

The run command emits an event for the start, the success, and the failure of each mint and refresh action. It also emits events for child spawn, child exit, signal receipt, and signal forwarding. The other commands build the same events but discard them because they install no emitter.
The system writes all events to standard error and never to standard output. In run mode standard output belongs to the child alone.

No call site writes a credential value into an event. The token field carries a plain token identifier. No type or function prevents a caller from writing a secret into the token field or the error field.
The log format parser accepts only the lowercase words json and text. It rejects every other value, including any other capitalization.
Every failure that the Error type carries names one category from a closed set of six. The categories are usage, config, provider, security, profile, and internal.
Each error category maps to one fixed process exit code. Usage and security give 64. Provider gives 65. Profile gives 66. Internal gives 70. Config gives 78. Success gives 0.

When a command returns an error and the operator selected JSON output, main writes one JSON object to standard error. The object carries the status, the command name, the error kind, and the message. In text mode main writes one line that starts with noscope and a colon.
The validate, dry-run, mint, revoke, and init commands write their success message to standard output. These five commands write nothing to standard error when they succeed.
In JSON output mode the dry-run, validate, and revoke commands each write one JSON object to standard output. Each object carries an ok status, the command name, and the provider.

When a revoke command fails, the failure message that reaches the operator includes the text that the provider wrote to standard error. The mint path discards provider standard error and reports the exit code alone.
The completions command writes a shell completion script to standard output. It accepts every shell that the completion library defines, which includes bash, zsh, and fish.

The binary hands help output, version output, and argument parse errors to the argument parser, which prints them and exits. The parser writes help and version text to standard output and exits 0. It writes a usage error and exits 2.
Help text speaks to operators. It carries concrete run, mint, and revoke examples. It explains that the profile flag excludes the credential flags. It never shows internal rule identifiers.
The failure codes in the NoscopeExitCode set start at 64 and never collide with the provider protocol codes 1 to 4. The doctor command and the argument parser return values outside that set.
The product must not present a safety behaviour as working when it does not yet hold. The operator documentation separates the behaviour that works today from the behaviour that remains planned.
The system rests on three safety layers. These are process group termination, revocation at exit, and expiry by TTL.
A failed credential refresh never stops the child process. Noscope retries the refresh with growing delays. After the retries run out noscope lets the credential expire on its own.

Refresh retries start at 1 second and double on each attempt. Noscope stops after 4 retries. Each retry delay varies by up to 25 percent. Noscope skips a retry whose delay exceeds half of the credential lifetime that remains.
Noscope tracks refresh failures separately for each credential. A failure on one credential never changes the retry state of another credential.
A run of failed refreshes never disables refresh for good. The credential returns to its normal refresh time after the failure window. The next attempt always waits at least 1 second.
Noscope runs a refresh command only for credentials whose refresh time has arrived. Noscope runs no refresh command after the child process exits.

A provider refresh command receives the current credential value and the credential identifier. The command also receives the credential lifetime in whole seconds. The provider uses these values to renew that exact lease.

Noscope warns at startup whenever rotate mode is active. The warning states that noscope injects environment variables once at spawn time. The warning states that the running child never sees a refreshed credential.

Noscope computes a refresh time for each credential from that credential's own expiry. The refresh time falls at 75 percent of the granted lifetime. Noscope never merges credentials into one shared schedule.
The expiry of one credential must not stop the child process. The expiry must not trigger a new mint. Noscope must warn the operator and name the provider and the token identifier.
Every failed refresh produces a warning for the operator. Noscope emits that warning even when it still plans a retry.
Choose the revoke contract: identifier-only or token-in-env.

Ratify or reject the asymmetry: run mode rolls back succeeded credentials on partial mint failure, mint mode does not.
Decide ship-or-delete for the unwired refresh subsystem before the rewrite; its twelve landed obligations describe designed, unshipped behaviour.

proposals.title: cross exit namespaces disjoint
proposals.summary: The failure codes in the NoscopeExitCode set start at 64 and never collide with the provider protocol codes 1 to 4. The doctor command and the argument parser return values outside that set. Known gaps: a child process may still exit 1-4 or 64-78 and be indistinguishable Adversarial notes: Values live at src/exit_code.rs:99. The contested point stands: a child process may still exit with any value in either range, and the run path passes that value through unchanged at src/main.rs:404.

proposals.title: docs implemented vs planned
proposals.summary: The product must not present a safety behaviour as working when it does not yet hold. The operator documentation separates the behaviour that works today from the behaviour that remains planned. Adversarial notes: Sites: README.md:88 to README.md:98, docs/QUICKSTART.md:82 to docs/QUICKSTART.md:93, and the lint at tests/noscope_3ez_7_docs.rs:70. Treat the string-matching test as a process artifact and keep the honesty obligation as the requirement.

proposals.title: docs three safety layers
proposals.summary: The system rests on three safety layers. These are process group termination, revocation at exit, and expiry by TTL. Known gaps: matches the coverage findings — group termination is unwired and revoke-on-exit has gaps Adversarial notes: The architecture claim belongs to the product, so it survives, but no cited evidence is code. Supporting code does exist and should replace the prose evidence: src/process_group.rs:40 for the new group and the parent death signal, src/agent_process.rs:162 for group signalling, and src/main.rs:401 for revoke on child exit. One genuine gap: process_group::terminate_group_for_mode at src/process_group.rs:32 has no production caller, so only the signal-forwarding route reaches the group.

proposals.title: refresh never kills child
proposals.summary: src/refresh.rs:RefreshPolicy implements: A failed credential refresh never stops the child process. Noscope retries the refresh with growing delays. After the retries run out noscope lets the credential expire on its own. Known gaps: UNWIRED — cmd_run never constructs RefreshRuntimeLoop. Applies to every refresh cluster Adversarial notes: Verified. RefreshPolicy::on_refresh_failure at src/refresh.rs:140-175 returns only Retry or AllowExpiry. KillChild is unreachable by construction, so the exhaustive attempts 0-100 test at src/refresh.rs:927 is tautological and proves nothing beyond the enum shape. The obligation itself is durable and belongs in the graph regardless of shipping, so keep as a rule with the unwired caveat that cmd_run never builds RefreshRuntimeLoop.

proposals.title: refresh retry params
proposals.summary: src/refresh.rs:RetryParams implements: Refresh retries start at 1 second and double on each attempt. Noscope stops after 4 retries. Each retry delay varies by up to 25 percent. Noscope skips a retry whose delay exceeds half of the credential lifetime that remains. Known gaps: UNWIRED | the half-lifetime check is per attempt not cumulative | max_retry_window clamps its own result so its bound test cannot fail Adversarial notes: The thresholds at src/refresh.rs:57-66 are real defaults that a future provider author would observe, so keep the cluster as a rule. The cumulative half-lifetime budget should enter the graph as a separate unmet obligation rather than as described behaviour. The xorshift jitter source at src/refresh.rs:533 is an internal mechanic and should not enter the graph.

proposals.title: refresh per credential isolation
proposals.summary: src/refresh.rs:RefreshTracker implements: Noscope tracks refresh failures separately for each credential. A failure on one credential never changes the retry state of another credential. Known gaps: UNWIRED Adversarial notes: Verified at src/refresh.rs:232, where RuntimeCredential::new builds one RefreshTracker per credential, and by the test at src/refresh.rs:808. The RefreshTracker struct shape is a detail, but the isolation obligation is durable: one provider outage must not shrink another provider's retry budget. A human weighing ship or delete needs this in the graph. Keep with the unwired caveat.

proposals.title: refresh never disabled for good
proposals.summary: src/refresh.rs:record_refresh_failure implements: A run of failed refreshes never disables refresh for good. The credential returns to its normal refresh time after the failure window. The next attempt always waits at least 1 second. Known gaps: UNWIRED | failure count grows across windows unless a success arrives Adversarial notes: The scheduling half is real. record_refresh_failure sets next_refresh_at through normal_refresh_at at src/refresh.rs:475-482, which floors the wait at 1 second and prevents a tight loop. I dropped the retry-budget-reset half because no code performs it. Keep as a rule with the unwired caveat.

proposals.title: refresh due only child alive
proposals.summary: src/refresh.rs:run_once implements: Noscope runs a refresh command only for credentials whose refresh time has arrived. Noscope runs no refresh command after the child process exits. Known gaps: UNWIRED Adversarial notes: Verified at src/refresh.rs:329 for the child gate and src/refresh.rs:336 for the due filter. No NS rule in .beads/provenance-drafts backs this, but it is a durable safety obligation: a dead child needs no fresh credential, and refreshing past child life extends a live secret for nobody. Two weaknesses to record against the rule. child_alive is a flag the caller supplies and the loop never observes the process itself. The loop checks the flag once per tick, so a child that exits during a tick still gets the rest of that tick's refreshes.

proposals.title: refresh request carries lease
proposals.summary: A provider refresh command receives the current credential value and the credential identifier. The command also receives the credential lifetime in whole seconds. The provider uses these values to renew that exact lease. Known gaps: UNWIRED | the request holds the raw secret as a plain String outside the secret wrapper Adversarial notes: Keep as a requirement because a provider author writes a refresh script against this env contract, and that contract exists today in provider_exec even though the refresh loop does not. Separate security finding worth its own entry: RefreshExecutionRequest at src/refresh.rs:248 derives Debug and stores token_value as a plain String copied out of the secret wrapper at src/refresh.rs:353. Any debug print of the request leaks the token, which conflicts with the NS-005 redaction rule.

proposals.title: refresh rotate mode warning
proposals.summary: src/refresh.rs:rotate_mode_startup_warning implements: Noscope warns at startup whenever rotate mode is active. The warning states that noscope injects environment variables once at spawn time. The warning states that the running child never sees a refreshed credential. Known gaps: UNWIRED and no rotate mode flag exists Adversarial notes: Verified at src/refresh.rs:183-188 for the text and src/refresh.rs:282-287 for the once-only startup emission. Confirmed that src/cli.rs defines no rotate or refresh flag, so the rule is vacuously satisfied today. Keep it anyway. This is the strongest reason to question shipping the whole feature, because environment injection cannot deliver a refreshed credential to a running child. A human deciding ship or delete must see this obligation first.

proposals.title: refresh schedule 75pct
proposals.summary: src/credential_set.rs:compute_refresh_at implements: Noscope computes a refresh time for each credential from that credential's own expiry. The refresh time falls at 75 percent of the granted lifetime. Noscope never merges credentials into one shared schedule. Known gaps: 75 percent of remaining-at-call-time, so repeated calls drift later | an expired token yields a past refresh time with no stated handler Adversarial notes: Keep as a rule. The 75 percent point is a threshold a provider author would observe and a human would argue about, unlike the tracker internals. State the rule against the granted lifetime, which is the clear intent of NS-048, and carry the remaining-time drift as a defect against the rule rather than as the rule itself.

proposals.title: refresh expiry log only
proposals.summary: src/credential_set.rs:ExpiryPolicy implements: The expiry of one credential must not stop the child process. The expiry must not trigger a new mint. Noscope must warn the operator and name the provider and the token identifier. Known gaps: UNWIRED — nothing in the live run loop watches expiry at all, so even the warning never reaches an operator Adversarial notes: Keep the two prohibitions as a rule, because they mirror the never-kills-child rule and a human would want both before deciding to ship or delete. Record the warning as a required behaviour that no code path performs. Note the same negative-constraint pattern as RefreshAction::KillChild: ExpiryAction::TerminateChild and ExpiryAction::ReMint exist at src/credential_set.rs:222 only so tests can assert against them.

proposals.title: refresh failure warning always
proposals.summary: Every failed refresh produces a warning for the operator. Noscope emits that warning even when it still plans a retry. Known gaps: UNWIRED and nothing writes the warning text Adversarial notes: Verified that all four return paths of on_refresh_failure set log_warning to true at src/refresh.rs:143-174, and that run_once emits a RefreshFail event at src/refresh.rs:377. Keep as a requirement, because suppressing retry noise is a real design choice and this states the opposite of it. Caveat to carry: no code reads outcome.log_warning outside tests, so the flag is a promise rather than an emitted warning.

proposals.title: which revoke contract is intended
proposals.summary: Choose one revoke contract. Side A: revocation works from the credential identifier alone and the provider contract drops NOSCOPE_TOKEN. Side B: the binary carries the raw credential to the revoke command as the drafted NS-038 contract states. The losing implementation must be deleted. The two contested proposals backtrace/token/revoke-by-id-only and backtrace/exec/revoke-env-contract carry the evidence for each side.

evidence_references.summary: execute_revoke passes an empty NOSCOPE_TOKEN and only the token id
build_revoke_env sets NOSCOPE_TOKEN and NOSCOPE_TOKEN_ID per the drafted provider contract
the public library runtime passes token.expose_secret() where the binary passes an empty string
NS-038 drafts the contract as NOSCOPE_TOKEN plus NOSCOPE_TOKEN_ID
prior review rates the mismatch high severity and lists the same fork as an open question

synthesis_packets.summary: Follow-up adjudication after the human decision on the revoke-contract fork. Ben chose identifier-only revocation on 2026-08-18, recorded as resolution res_revoke_contract_identifier_only. The formerly contested claim clm_token-revoke-by-id-only is adjudicated here so the winning proposal can carry its assertion. The losing proposal prop_exec-revoke-env-contract was rejected by disposition.

consensus.statement: The noscope binary revokes a credential using the credential identifier and the provider name alone, and this is the chosen contract.

open_questions: The rewrite must delete the token-carrying revoke path in integration_runtime and drop NOSCOPE_TOKEN as a value channel from the provider contract.

suggested_artifacts.summary: Identifier-only revocation, chosen side of the revoke-contract fork.
